records.briefDescription: A high guard with the sword held above the head (or resting on the shoulder), the point extending upward, serving as Meyer's principal upper guard (Oberhut, 'From the Day') and the main launching point for descending cuts.
records.fullDescription:
Stand with the sword held on your right shoulder (or above your head), with the blade angled approximately 45 degrees backward and upward. Your hands should be near your temple or above your head, with your weight distributed to enable a powerful forward step. The point aims back-right, creating potential energy for descending cuts. From this position, your forearms may be crossed or uncrossed depending on which side you hold it.

This guard exemplifies maximum potential energy—like a coiled spring ready to release. The blade can rest on the shoulder or be held slightly off it. Your body should be slightly coiled, ready to unwind into a powerful strike. Meyer treats Vom Tag not as a static hold but as a transitional 'moment in motion'—the outermost point reached as you lift the sword for a high cut, from which you immediately strike.
records.fullApplication:
Use Vom Tag as your primary launching point for descending cuts, especially the Zornhau (Wrath Cut). This guard excels at seizing the initiative (the Vor) by threatening the opponent's upper openings with powerful overhead strikes. It's particularly effective when you need to break through an opponent's guard with sheer force and forward pressure.

Enter with this guard when you want to dominate the high line and force your opponent to react defensively. The guard is countered by the Zwerchhau—Meyer's own verse says the Crosswise Cut "can counteract everything that comes from the Day"—so be prepared to commit fully to your attack or transition quickly if your opponent employs this counter. Vom Tag is your go-to position when you need maximum striking power and want to establish psychological dominance through an overtly aggressive posture.
records.briefApplication: Use Vom Tag as your primary launching point for descending cuts, especially the Zornhau (Wrath Cut).

records.briefDescription: A deceptive low guard with hands extended forward and point dropped toward the ground, designed to bait the opponent into attacking your deliberately exposed upper openings.
records.fullDescription:
Hold your sword with arms extended forward, hands at approximately waist to hip height, with the point lowered toward the ground at roughly a 45-degree angle. The sword is held on the centerline of your body (or slightly to one side), with the quillons near your lead forearm. The guard appears passive and vulnerable, with your upper body seemingly undefended—this is intentional. Your body posture should be slightly coiled despite the extended arms, ready to spring upward.

The name 'Fool' (Alber, 'simpleminded') reflects the apparently foolish exposure of the openings; as Meyer notes, no proper stroke can readily be made from this guard, so it serves chiefly to provoke and to parry rather than to attack. It marks the lowest point of the descending vertical line (Day, then Longpoint, then Fool), from which you gather for a new cut after catching the opponent's blade.
records.fullApplication:
Use Alber as a provoking guard to bait your opponent into attacking your high openings. When they commit to a descending strike, rapidly rise into a hanging parry (Hengetort) or transition through Pflug to thrust upward into their attack. The guard is specifically designed to draw overcommitted attacks that you can intercept or slip under.

Alber is countered by the Scheitelhau (Scalp Cut), which drives down over the top against your lowered point and threatens the head—so if you see it coming, transition immediately. This guard teaches you to appear vulnerable, invite the attack, and then use the opponent's committed energy against them. It's particularly effective against aggressive opponents who can't resist an apparently open target.
records.briefApplication: Use Alber as a provoking guard to bait your opponent into attacking your high openings.

records.briefDescription: A high thrusting guard with the hilt held near the temple and the point extending forward toward the opponent's face like the horns of an ox.
records.fullDescription:
Hold your hilt next to your head at temple level, with the point directed toward your opponent's eyes or throat. When holding Ochs on your right side (Meyer stands here with the left foot forward), your forearms are not crossed; on your left side they cross. You can use either a handshake grip (with quillons nearly vertical and true edge upward) or a thumb grip (with quillons nearly horizontal and thumb underneath). The blade is angled roughly 30-45 degrees forward from vertical. This guard is also called the 'upper hengen' (upper hanging).

Your stance should be mobile, with weight ready to press forward behind the thrust. The point must always threaten the opponent's face or upper chest—this is critical to the guard's function. Meyer treats Ochs as a transitional position rather than a static hold, always ready to wind or strike. The hands are high and relatively protected by the blade's angle. This guard exists on either side of the body, creating four total variations when combined with Pflug.
records.fullApplication:
Use Ochs as your primary high-line thrusting platform and as a strong binding position from which to wind and work in the Krieg (the war—close-range blade work). Ochs excels at maintaining constant offensive pressure with the threat of an immediate thrust while also being ready to catch and bind incoming strikes. From here, you can quickly thrust, execute a Zwerchhau, or wind into various actions based on what you feel (fühlen) in the bind.

Ochs is particularly effective after catching an opponent's strike, as it naturally positions you for winding actions. The guard is broken by Krumphau (Crooked Cut), which specifically targets this position by coming over your blade to strike your hands or head. When in Ochs, always be prepared to wind or strike through, never remain static. This guard shines when you need to combine defense and offense simultaneously, threatening while protecting. The 'Vier Hengen' (four hangings) system uses Ochs and Pflug as the primary positions for winding work.
records.briefApplication: Use Ochs as your primary high-line thrusting platform and as a strong binding position from which to wind and work in the Krieg (the war—close-range blade work).

records.briefDescription: A low thrusting guard with hands positioned near the hip and the point directed forward on the centerline toward the opponent's face or chest.
records.fullDescription:
Hold your hilt next to your hip (right or left), with the point directed toward your opponent's eyes or throat along the centerline. When holding Pflug on your right, your forearms are not crossed; on your left they cross. You can use either a handshake grip (quillons nearly vertical with true edge downward) or a thumb grip (quillons nearly horizontal with thumb on top). Your hands should be at hip to waist height, with the blade angled upward approximately 30-45 degrees so the point threatens the upper body. This is called the 'lower hengen' (lower hanging).

Your body should be in a stable, rooted stance that can drive forward behind the thrust. The low hand position protects your hands while the point remains a constant threat. Meyer treats Pflug as a transitional thrusting position rather than a static hold, ready to thrust or wind instantly. Like Ochs, Pflug exists on both sides, contributing to the four hangings that form the core of winding work.
records.fullApplication:
Use Pflug as your primary low-line thrusting position and as a safe platform from which to enter combat or recover after landing a hit. Pflug excels at controlling the centerline while keeping your hands protected and low. From this position, you can thrust directly, rise into cuts, or wind into various upper or lower attacks based on pressure in the bind.

Pflug is particularly valuable for defensive recovery—many instructors recommend pulling back to Pflug after landing a hit to protect against afterblows, as your hands are low and safe while your point still threatens. The guard is broken by Schielhau (Squinting Cut), which specifically displaces Pflug's point while striking. Use Pflug when you need a stable, patient position that maintains threat while protecting your hands.

It's excellent for testing the opponent's commitment—maintain Pflug and see how they react, then wind or thrust based on what you feel. The combination of Pflug and Ochs creates the complete hengen system from which all winding actions emerge. Pflug is also ideal for setting up Durchwechseln (changing through) if the opponent binds onto your blade.
records.briefApplication: Use Pflug as your primary low-line thrusting position and as a safe platform from which to enter combat or recover after landing a hit.

records.briefDescription: A fully extended guard position with arms straightened and the point aimed directly at the opponent, creating maximum reach and an immediate linear threat.
records.fullDescription:
Extend both arms fully forward (without locking your elbows) with the point of your sword aimed directly at your opponent's face, throat, or chest. Your blade should form a straight line from your hands to the target. Your weight should be balanced, with your lead foot forward and your body positioned to drive behind the thrust if needed. The sword's quillons should align with your lead forearm for proper structure and hand protection.

This position is sometimes called Sprechfenster (Speaking Window) when specifically used to maintain contact and 'feel' the opponent's pressure in the bind. Langort is essentially the extended version of both Ochs and Pflug—it's where many techniques naturally end after a thrust or parry. Your point should remain steady and on target, creating a barrier the opponent must deal with before they can reach you. The position should feel strong and rooted through your core, with the blade acting as an extension of your arms. This is the most linear and direct of all guards.
records.fullApplication:
Use Langort to control distance and deny your opponent the ability to attack freely. This guard excels at maintaining the Vor (initiative) by presenting a constant, immediate threat that forces your opponent to react before they can launch their own attacks. Langort is the common ending position after executing Absetzen (setting aside)—you parry by extending into long point, simultaneously defending and threatening.

It's also valuable when you need to gauge your opponent's intentions through blade contact (fühlen) without committing to a specific technique. From Langort/Sprechfenster, you can feel whether your opponent is hard or soft, then immediately wind, thrust, or strike based on that information. Use this guard when you've landed a thrust and want to maintain pressure, or when you need to control the measure and tempo of the fight. The extended point makes it difficult for opponents to rush in with close-range techniques without first dealing with your threat.

Langort is particularly effective in the transition between the Zufechten (the onset) and the Handarbeit (the middle, or 'handwork'), as it bridges distance control with binding options.
records.briefApplication: Use Langort to control distance and deny your opponent the ability to attack freely.

records.briefDescription: A low, sunken guard with the hilt held before the knee and the point angled upward toward the opponent's face, forming a protective 'iron gate' from which cuts and thrusts can be turned aside.
records.fullDescription:
Stand with your right foot forward and hold your sword with the hilt in front of your knee, your arms hanging straight down, so that the point extends upward and out toward your opponent's face. Stand with your feet wide so that your body sinks low; from this sunken position you can carry away all cuts and thrusts directed at you, holding the sword before you for defense 'like an iron gate.' The point is up and forward (roughly between Pflug and Langort), not down—this is what distinguishes the true Eisenport.

Meyer notes that because thrusting with the sword had largely fallen out of use among the Germans of his day, this guard had declined, though the Italians and other nations still used it. He observes that the inexperienced, lacking knowledge of the Eisenport, tend to substitute the Schrankhut (crossed hands, point on the ground) for it; the two are related but distinct. He treats the Iron Gate more fully in his Rapier section.
records.fullApplication:
Use Eisenport as a strong, covering guard: sinking low behind the sword, you can turn aside descending cuts and thrusts and answer with a thrust or cut up into your opponent's face or openings, since the point already sits forward and up toward him. It is a defensive, space-holding posture from which you drive the point forward rather than a chamber for big cuts.

Meyer himself remarks that the guard had fallen into decline among Germans because thrusting with the longsword had been set aside, and that it belongs more to the thrust-oriented play he details in the Rapier. Treat it as a specialized, somewhat old-fashioned covering guard—useful for holding a firm barrier and threatening the thrust—rather than one of the four principal guards (Ochs, Pflug, vom Tag, Alber) from which Meyer's core longsword play flows. Do not confuse it with the Schrankhut, which the untrained often use in its place.
records.briefApplication: Use Eisenport as a strong covering guard, sinking low behind the sword to turn aside cuts and thrusts while threatening a thrust up into the opponent's face.

records.briefDescription: A guard with the arms extended forward in front of the face and the point hanging down toward the ground, like the Ox but with the arms held out straight rather than high, used to intercept strikes and wind into thrusts.
records.fullDescription:
Stand with your right foot forward and hold your sword with your arms extended forward, straight out in front of your face, so that the blade hangs somewhat downward toward the earth. Meyer says this stance is almost identical to the Ox, except that in the Ox you hold the arms high up in the air, whereas here they should be stretched out level in front of your face while the sword hangs toward the ground—which is why it is called the Hanging Point. The true edge generally faces toward the opponent's blade so as to catch a strike cleanly.

Your body should be poised to extend or wind immediately on contact: the hanging point means that once you catch a strike, you need only turn your hands forward and straighten your arms to bring the point into a thrust. Though it looks defensive, it carries immediate offensive potential through winding, and it can be held on either side and adjusted to the angle of the incoming attack.
records.fullApplication:
Use Hengetort primarily to intercept and parry descending strikes (Oberhau) while simultaneously preparing to thrust or cut in response. This guard works in the Nach (the responsive role): when your opponent throws an overhead attack, you catch their blade on your strong while your point hangs ready, then wind your hands forward and straighten your arms to deliver a thrust to their face or body, using their committed energy against them.

Because it is essentially the Ox with the arms extended forward and the point lowered, it flows naturally into the winding and hanging actions Meyer builds on the Ox. Unlike a purely defensive parry, Hengetort lets you seize the initiative through winding the instant blades meet.

Use this guard when you expect descending attacks, when you want to play responsively but counter instantly, or when an overhead attack materializes as you transition through a high guard. The guard can be held on either side and adjusted based on the angle of the incoming attack.
records.briefApplication: Use Hengetort primarily to intercept and parry overhead strikes (Oberhau) while simultaneously preparing to thrust or cut in response.

records.briefDescription: An extended guard position with the point directed forward in front of your face, used to maintain blade contact and 'speak' with the opponent through pressure (fühlen) while threatening constantly.
records.fullDescription:
Extend your arms forward with your hands in front of or slightly below your face and the point aimed at your opponent's face or upper chest, the sword nearly fully extended into a straight line of threat. In practice this is Langort brought into contact with the opponent's blade: you rest lightly on or against their sword so that you can feel their pressure and read their intentions. Meyer lists Sprechfenster among his secondary guards (Beyleger), but it functions less as a fixed static posture than as the moment in the bind where you 'speak' with your opponent through the blade.

The name means 'speaking window': you 'lie in the speaking window,' remain on the bind, and mark what your opponent intends before committing. Keep the position active and alert rather than static, using it to gather information through feeling (fühlen) while holding a constant threat with the point. Your weight should be distributed to allow instant forward or circular movement so you can wind, thrust, or cut the moment you feel an opening.
records.fullApplication:
Use Sprechfenster in the Handarbeit—the middle or 'handwork' of the bout, where the blades meet—to maintain contact with your opponent's blade while reading their pressure and intentions through fühlen. This position excels at the moment of engagement when blades are touching but neither fencer has committed to a specific technique. From it you can immediately wind to thrust high or low, cut around their blade, or maintain pressure based on whether they are hard (strong) or soft (weak) in the bind. The 'speaking' metaphor is key—you hold a conversation through steel, asking questions with pressure and reading the answers through feeling.

Use Sprechfenster when you have engaged the opponent's blade but need to assess before committing to your next action. It is particularly valuable when both fighters enter and create a bind at once, letting you gather intelligence while maintaining threat. The point on the centerline denies your opponent the chance to rush in with grappling or close-range techniques.

Because Sprechfenster is essentially Langort brought to bear in the bind, wind from it based on what you feel: if they are soft, thrust through; if they are hard, wind around; if they pull away, follow with Nachreisen.
records.briefApplication: Use Sprechfenster in the Handarbeit (the middle, or 'handwork,' of the bind) to maintain contact with your opponent's blade while reading their pressure and intentions through fühlen.

records.briefDescription: A guard with the hilt and crossed hands held before the chest, the short edge resting on the left arm and the point directed forward at the opponent's face, threatening the thrust while shutting the high line.
records.fullDescription:
Stand with your left foot forward and hold your sword with the hilt and crossed hands in front of your chest, so that the short (false) edge rests on top of your left arm and the point extends forward toward your opponent's face. The crossed-hand structure braces the blade across the front of your body, closing the high line while keeping the point online as a standing threat. Meyer illustrates it in the figure marked D.

Keep the arms supported and the point steady on your opponent's face. From the Key the hands are already set to wind: it is the base position from which Meyer forms the Unicorn (Einhorn)—you simply wing the elbows out and lift the crossed hands up to your right so the point rises. The guard should feel braced and forward-threatening rather than withdrawn, controlling the center with a covered, point-forward structure.
records.fullApplication:
Use Schlüssel to shut down your opponent's high attacks while keeping your own point online: the crossed hands and covered blade let you catch or bar a descending strike, and the point stays aimed at the face so you can answer immediately with a thrust. It is a guard of closing and threatening at once—you occupy the center and dare your opponent to work around a covered point.

Because the hands are already crossed and braced, the Key flows directly into winding and into the Unicorn (Einhorn): lift the crossed hands up to your right and the point rises into a high threat, or wind to thrust as the pressure in the bind dictates. Use it when you want to hold a strong forward barrier before turning it into a thrust or a winding attack.

Don't remain in Schlüssel statically—like a key, its purpose is to turn: brace the line, then unlock it into a thrust, a wind, or a rise into the Unicorn as the opening appears.
records.briefApplication: Use Schlüssel to close your opponent's high line with covered, crossed hands while keeping your point aimed at their face for an immediate thrust or wind.

records.briefDescription: A high guard reached by winging the crossed hands up to the right so the point stands upward and outward toward the opponent's face—essentially the Ox with the point angled higher.
records.fullDescription:
Come into the Onset with your left foot forward, wing your elbows out to both sides as if setting into the Key (Schlüssel), then lift your crossed hands upward to your right so that the point extends outward and upward toward your opponent's face. This is the Unicorn (Meyer shows it in the figure marked E). It resembles the Ox, but where the Ox holds the point roughly level toward the face, the Unicorn carries the hands and point higher so the blade angles upward like a single horn.

Keep the crossed-hand structure that lets you wind and thrust immediately. Because you arrive in it by flinging the hands up from the Key, the Unicorn is a mobile, transitional high guard as much as a static posture—it stands ready to drop a strike, wind, or thrust down onto the opponent from above.
records.briefApplication: Use Einhorn as a high, point-forward threat from which to thrust or wind down onto the opponent, especially after winging up out of a bind or the Key.
records.fullApplication:
Use the Unicorn to threaten from a high, crossed-hand position: with the point angled up and out toward your opponent's face, you can thrust down into the upper openings or wind against pressure in the bind, much as you would from the Ox. Meyer reaches it dynamically—winging the hands up into the Unicorn during the Onset or out of a bind (for instance in his Squinter play), so that from the raised crossed hands you cut or thrust down with the short edge onto the opponent's blade, arms, or head.

Because it is essentially the Ox with the point carried higher, treat it as a launching point for downward thrusts, winds, and short-edge strikes rather than a guard to sit in. Use it to seize a high, covering line and immediately convert it into an attack from above, and flow between it and the Key as the play demands.

records.briefDescription: A low guard held beside the right with the point resting toward the ground and the pommel upward, from which you can sweep upward or across into rising and horizontal strikes.
records.fullDescription:
Stand with your left foot forward and hold your sword beside your right side with the point down toward the ground, so that the pommel is upward and the short edge faces toward you. (This is Meyer's longsword Side Guard; in his Dußack he sets a Side Guard by the left hip with the point to the rear, but in the longsword it sits low on the right with the point down.) Your body turns slightly to present a narrow profile, and the guard looks withdrawn and passive while holding potential energy for a rising or crosswise strike.

Your stance should be coiled, weight ready to drive forward as the blade sweeps up and across the opponent's line. Because the point starts low and to the side, you uncoil through a large arc to strike, which telegraphs the target less than a high guard since the blade must travel regardless of where you aim. It is close kin to the Change (Wechsel), which sits low on the same side—the difference is chiefly the foot forward and the edge orientation.
records.fullApplication:
Use Nebenhut to invite your opponent to commit to an attack on your apparently open upper openings, then answer with a powerful rising or crosswise strike driven by full body rotation. This guard excels at baiting and countering: your low, withdrawn position tempts an aggressive opponent to strike, giving you the chance to sweep up and across with an Unterhau (rising strike) or a Zwerchhau (thwart strike) from below their line. The narrow profile you present makes you a harder target.

Meyer's plays from the Side Guard repeatedly take the opponent's incoming cut or thrust by 'taking out' with a hanging deflection and then cutting or thrusting back—so treat it as a receiving and countering position as much as a baiting one. Use it to reset the tempo or to change the character of the fight by withdrawing briefly.

Don't overuse this guard, as holding it too long surrenders the initiative (Vor). Use it as a brief provocation or a transitional moment before exploding into action; the large sweeping arcs it allows generate significant power through body mechanics.
records.briefApplication: Use Nebenhut when you want to invite the opponent to commit to an attack on your apparently open side, then respond with a powerful rising or crosswise strike that uses maximum body rotation.

records.briefDescription: A low guard held with crossed hands in front of the body and the point resting on the ground, forming a barred cross in front of you to catch cuts and thrusts before rising into a counter.
records.fullDescription:
Stand with the sword held in crossed hands in front of your body with the point down on the ground, forming a low barrier (Meyer illustrates it in the figure marked F). The crossed-hand structure bars the line in front of you, and because the point is grounded you sit behind a solid cover rather than a diagonal high-to-low guard. It can be set on either side, and the low, sunken posture lets you carry incoming cuts and thrusts aside.

Meyer treats the Schrankhut (the 'Crossed Guard') as closely related to the Eisenport: he notes that the inexperienced, lacking knowledge of the true Iron Gate, commonly use the Schrankhut in its place. The difference is that the Eisenport holds the point up and forward toward the face, while in the Schrankhut the crossed hands set the point down on the ground. Keep the posture braced and ready to rise, wind, or slice as your opponent commits.
records.fullApplication:
Use Schrankhut as a low, barred cover: from behind the crossed hands you catch or carry away your opponent's cuts and thrusts, then rise, wind, or slice into your counter as they commit. Sinking low behind the grounded point gives you a firm barrier against attacks to the lower openings, and the crossed structure lets you displace strongly to either side.

Because Meyer links it to the Eisenport, treat it much as you would that guard: a defensive, space-holding posture from which you answer with a thrust or a rising cut rather than a chamber for large blows. It suits opponents who press with cuts, since you meet them behind a solid cross and immediately work out of the bind.

Don't remain static in this guard; use it to receive and cover, then rise or wind out of it into your attack. It works well combined with footwork that drives the cross forward into the opponent's space as you displace their strike.
records.briefApplication: Use Schrankhut as a low, barred cover: catch or carry away the opponent's cuts and thrusts behind the crossed hands, then rise, wind, or slice into your counter.

records.briefDescription: A high guard held at the right shoulder with the blade hanging down behind, showing 'wrathful' body language; from it Meyer says you can fence everything that comes from the Ox, using the different posture to deceive your opponent.
records.fullDescription:
Stand with your left foot forward and hold your sword at your right shoulder so that the blade hangs down behind you, ready for the planned strike. The guard is named for the wrathful bearing it shows: Meyer says the posture displays an angry body language that both threatens and misleads. Your hands sit at the right shoulder and the point falls back and down behind you, loading a strong descending strike.

Meyer notes that every sequence you can bring from the guard of the Ox can also be fenced from the Wrath Guard—the value of the stance is that it presents a dissimilar body language, so you can mislead your opponent and use now this guard, now the other. Keep the body poised over your feet rather than heavily rear-weighted; the posture should read as aggressive and ready to release either the strong descending Wrath Cut or the same plays you would make from the Ox.
records.fullApplication:
Use Zornhut when you want to threaten a powerful descending diagonal strike and to show aggressive intent that forces your opponent to respect it. From the right shoulder you can drive the Zornhau (Wrath Cut) straight into an opponent who opens the upper line, seizing the initiative (Vor), or meet an incoming Oberhau by cutting wrathfully into it and then working out of the bind.

Meyer's key point is that the Wrath Guard is interchangeable in its plays with the Ox: anything you would do from the Ox—winding, thrusting, cutting to the openings—you can also set up from here, but with a different, 'wrathful' body language that deceives your opponent about your intentions. Alternate between this stance and the Ox to keep your opponent guessing.

Use it when facing another high guard, where a strong descending cut or a bind and wind is the natural exchange, and whenever you want to load an aggressive strike while concealing which line you will actually attack.
records.briefApplication: Use Zornleger/Zornhut specifically when you intend to launch a Zornhau or when you want to appear ready to do so as a threat.

records.briefDescription: A powerful diagonal descending strike from the right shoulder that serves as the primary technique for countering overhead attacks, establishing a strong bind, and initiating follow-up winding actions.
records.fullDescription:
Begin in Vom Tag or Zornhut position with your sword chambered on your right shoulder. Step forward with your right foot (for right-handed fencers) as you unwind your body, driving a powerful diagonal cut from high right to low left. The strike should target your opponent's upper left opening (their head or shoulder) with a descending diagonal path. Your arms should extend forward as your body rotates, creating maximum power through full-body mechanics rather than just arm strength. The true (long) edge leads the cut. As you strike, your hands should drive forward and down, passing through the target line.

When executed as a counter to an incoming Oberhau, your Zornhau should meet their blade in a strong bind—your strong (forte) against their weak (foible) if possible. The strike ends in a lower position, often in a variation of Wechsel or a lower hanging position. Your right foot should end forward, with your hips turned toward the point of blade contact. The key is forward pressure and commitment—this isn't a tentative strike but a powerful, decisive action. Don't telegraph by pulling back first; strike directly from the chamber position.
records.fullApplication:
Use Zornhau as your primary response when an opponent strikes at you from above (Oberhau) or when you want to seize initiative with a powerful diagonal attack. This strike excels at meeting force with force—by striking simultaneously with your opponent's overhead cut, you create a bind where you can assess their pressure (hard or soft) through fühlen. If they're soft in the bind, immediately thrust along their blade to their face (Zornhau-Ort). If they're hard and push your sword aside, use Duplieren (doubling over to the other side) if they're very strong, or Mutieren (mutating to a lower thrust) if they're moderately strong.

The Zornhau is foundational to the entire Liechtenauer system—it's the first master strike taught, and the follow-up techniques (winding, duplieren, mutieren) from the Zornhau bind apply to virtually all other situations in the system. Use this strike when you need to establish control through force and forward pressure. It specifically counters other Oberhau attacks and can break through uncommitted guards.

The Zornhau is not a technique for displacing guards (unlike the other master strikes)—it's a direct, powerful killing blow that happens to create excellent binding opportunities when met with resistance. Practice this strike extensively, as it teaches the fundamental principle of striking 'with the strength of the whole body' and establishes the bind from which all close-range work flows.
records.briefApplication: Use Zornhau as your primary response when an opponent strikes at you from above (Oberhau) or when you want to seize initiative with a powerful diagonal attack.

records.briefDescription: A crossing diagonal strike delivered with a forward diagonal step, driving the pommel underneath your top arm until your forearms cross, targeting the opponent's hands or striking over their blade to break Ochs guard.
records.fullDescription:
In Meyer's device begin in the Zornhut (Wrath Guard) with your left foot forward. As your opponent cuts down at you from above, step well out to the side with your right foot, away from his strike and toward his left, and drive a cut that crosses the direct line rather than descending straight down it. The key mechanical feature is driving your pommel underneath your forward arm so your hands and forearms physically cross (geschränkt)—this creates the 'crooked' or 'crossing' character. In Meyer the crossing cut leads with the long edge, coming in with crossed arms between his blade and his head, onto his arm. Your hands drive forward with the pommel underneath, hooking over or against the opponent's blade.

The strike targets the opponent's hands and forearms, or crosses over his blade to catch it and strike on to his arm or head. The wide sideways step carries you offline from his attack while letting you reach across. The strike ends with your arms crossed and the point forward, online toward the opponent in a crossed hanging position.
records.fullApplication:
Use Krumphau specifically to break Ochs guard or to disrupt any attack or guard where the opponent's blade is high and forward. This strike excels at displacing the opponent's sword while simultaneously striking—it's not just a parry or just an attack, but both unified into one action. When you see an opponent in Ochs threatening to thrust, execute Krumphau by striking across and over their blade, hooking it down and away while your strike continues to their hands or head. The diagonal stepping takes you offline from their thrust while your crossing action gives you mechanical advantage.

Use Krumphau early in the fight (from Zufechten) when you need to break through a prepared guard. The strike also works against Zornhau—if you catch them early in their strike, you can Krump against their blade and redirect it. The verse states 'Krump to the flats of the master if you wish to weaken them'—this means striking to the flat of their blade (not edge-to-edge) to gain better displacement. Target their hands whenever possible, as hand strikes are immediately fight-ending.

The crossed-arm position you end in can immediately transition to winding and thrusting. Don't overuse this strike from close range—it requires space and time to execute properly. Use it from approach distance with committed footwork.
records.briefApplication: Use Krumphau specifically to break Ochs guard or to disrupt any attack or guard where the opponent's blade is high and forward.

records.briefDescription: A high horizontal strike that cuts across the upper line to win control over the opponent's hands and head, typically delivered with the short edge from the right and long edge from the left.
records.fullDescription: Meyer counts this among his four chief cuts as the Mittel- or Zwerchhauw (Middle or Thwart Cut), the horizontal counterpart to the diagonal Zornhau. Execute a horizontal or slightly rising cut at head height, striking across your opponent's upper line. From the right side the strike travels with the short (false) edge leading—twist your hands as you strike from Vom Tag so the short edge rotates into the blow, with your thumb placed under the flat of the blade, your hands high and your point hanging slightly downward in a hanging Ochs-like structure. From the left side, strike with the long (true) edge leading. The strike should arc across horizontally, targeting the opponent's head, neck, or arms. Your hands drive across your body at approximately shoulder to head height, with the blade traveling in a flat or slightly rising path. As you strike, step forward and across to generate power and to position yourself advantageously. The strike often ends in an Ochs-like position on the opposite side from where it started. Your body rotation is critical—the power comes from unwinding your core, not just swinging your arms. The Zwerchhau can strike to all four openings successively by alternating sides and heights. Your hands should pass in front of your face as you strike, creating a natural defensive structure.
records.fullApplication:
Use Zwerchhau specifically to break Vom Tag guard and to dominate the high line by striking over or through the opponent's hands. This strike excels at stopping overhead cuts before they develop—if you see an opponent preparing to strike from above, a quick Zwerchhau catches their hands or head before they can complete their strike. The horizontal path allows you to strike while simultaneously creating a barrier that intercepts descending attacks.

Use Zwerchhau when you need to seize control of the high line quickly and decisively. The strike works particularly well as a counter to Vom Tag because it reaches the target (hands or head) via a shorter path than a descending strike. You can chain multiple Zwerchhau strikes together, alternating sides to attack all four openings in succession—high right, high left, low right, low left.

The strike is versatile: use it to attack directly, to intercept attacks, or to work in the bind. When used from the bind with proper winding, Zwerchhau becomes a powerful way to strike around the opponent's defense while maintaining blade contact. The historical verse emphasizes that Zwerchhau 'threatens strongly' and 'takes away' whatever comes from above. Practice delivering this strike with full body rotation for maximum power, and practice the hand rotation necessary to deliver the short edge effectively from the right side.
records.briefApplication: Use Zwerchhau specifically to break Vom Tag guard and to dominate the high line by striking over or through the opponent's hands.

records.briefDescription: A vertical descending cut aimed straight down at the crown of the head—where the hair parts—whose superior reach breaks the low Alber guard by striking over it to the head before the opponent can raise a defense.
records.fullDescription:
Execute a vertical downward strike directly to the top of your opponent's head—where the hair parts, hence 'parting strike' or 'scalp strike.' Begin from Vom Tag or a high position and drive straight down with the true edge, keeping the blade vertical or near-vertical throughout the strike. Your hands should drive forward and down along the centerline, with minimal lateral deviation. The strike should be fast and committed, using forward pressure to penetrate the opponent's structure.

As you strike, step forward to add body weight behind the blow. The strike ends in Alber position as your blade follows through. Your arms should extend fully downward, with your hands dropping low after impact. The key is the vertical path—unlike Zornhau which is diagonal, Scheitelhau descends straight down the centerline. Your body should remain square and centered as you strike, rather than rotating. The power comes from dropping your weight and driving through the target.
records.fullApplication:
Use Scheitelhau specifically to break Alber guard through the principle of 'Überlaufen' (overrunning/overreaching). When your opponent is in Alber with their point low, Scheitelhau drives vertically down onto their head, and if they try to rise to parry, your strike 'overruns' theirs—you hit them before they can get their point up. The vertical path makes this strike particularly effective against low guards because it arrives faster along the direct line than diagonal strikes.

Use Scheitelhau when you identify that your opponent favors Alber or other low positions. The strike forces them into a high parry position, which opens them to follow-up winding and thrusting techniques. After landing Scheitelhau (or after they parry it), you're in an excellent position to wind and thrust because your blade has driven them high and you can quickly mutate to a lower thrust.

The strike also works against other vertical preparations or when you want to attack directly down the centerline with maximum commitment. Be aware that Scheitelhau is less versatile than Zornhau or Zwerchhau—it's specifically an answer to low positions and to opponents who are slow to bring their defense up. The historical verse states it 'threatens the face' and is 'all to the top' emphasizing its direct, vertical nature. Practice this strike with proper edge alignment and sufficient power to penetrate through parrying attempts.
records.briefApplication: Use Scheitelhau specifically to break Alber guard through the principle of 'Überlaufen' (overrunning/overreaching).

records.briefDescription: An oblique diagonal strike that closes and displaces the opponent's thrusting line while simultaneously landing a blow, specifically designed to counter Pflug and other forward-pointing guards.
records.fullDescription:
Execute a diagonal descending strike with a twist—as you cut from Vom Tag, angle your strike to pass across the direct line while simultaneously displacing your opponent's blade. The name 'squinter' comes from the technique of looking at one target while striking at another, or looking down your blade as it angles across. Begin from Vom Tag on your right shoulder, step forward, and deliver a cut that descends diagonally but with your hands and blade angling to intercept and push aside the opponent's extended point as you strike.

The short edge typically leads this strike, delivered with a rotation of the hands. Your blade should simultaneously displace theirs offline while your edge continues through to strike their head or body. The footwork often involves stepping slightly offline to create an angle. Your strike essentially 'squints' across the line rather than traveling straight, creating both displacement and strike in one motion. The blade path might be described as coming from high right and cutting across toward their left side while pushing their weapon to your right.
records.fullApplication:
Use Schielhau specifically to break Pflug guard and to counter any position where your opponent's point is extended forward threatening to thrust. This strike excels at solving the problem of an extended point—rather than trying to parry first and then strike, Schielhau combines both actions into one motion. When your opponent is in Pflug or Langort, execute Schielhau by striking diagonally down while angling your blade to displace their point to the side, allowing your strike to land while their point is pushed offline.

Use this strike when facing thrusting guards or when opponents extend their point forward to maintain distance. The 'squinting' nature allows you to disguise your intention—you can look at one opening while your strike displaces and attacks another. The strike is versatile enough to work as both an opening attack in Zufechten and as a response to extended guards.

Historical sources note that Schielhau 'breaks' the long point and threatens the face. The strike also works against powerful Oberhau attacks—you can use Schielhau as a counter-strike that comes across their line, making it a valid response to multiple threats. Practice the hand rotation and blade angling that allows you to simultaneously displace and strike—this is more sophisticated than a simple cut and requires coordination of angle, edge, and timing.
records.briefApplication: Use Schielhau specifically to break Pflug guard and to counter any position where your opponent's point is extended forward threatening to thrust.

records.briefDescription: A flat-blade cut that rebounds off the opponent's blade or head and snaps back around for a renewed blow.
records.fullDescription: One of Meyer's inverted (verkehrt) longsword cuts, struck with the flat and using the bounce of the blade to chain blows. It comes in a single and a double form. Single: when the opponent cuts from above, meet the strike with a Zwerch (Crosswise); as soon as it glances off, pull the sword around your head and strike at their ear from your left with the outward, reversed flat so the blade rebounds back again, then pull that rebounding swing around your head once more and strike another Crosswise to the left. Double: as the opponent lifts the sword to work in the onset, stand in the right Ochs, pull the sword around your head and strike strongly with the inward flat against their blade so that your pommel touches near your forearm; as it glances, snap the reversed flat back around to the same opening, using the hard rebound to double the blow.
records.briefApplication: Use the Prellhau to chain flat-blade blows to the head and ears, exploiting the rebound to renew the attack before the opponent can recover.
records.fullApplication: A characteristically sportive Fechtschule cut that trades cutting power for speed and deception: because it lands with the flat it is well suited to friendly play, and the rebound lets you double a blow to the same opening or flow from one ear to the other faster than a normal recovery would allow. Use the single form after meeting an Oberhau with the Zwerch, and the double form from Ochs when the opponent raises to act, snapping repeated blows to the head while they are still occupied with the first.

records.briefDescription: A high descending cut that tips the point over and down so it drops into Ochs, threatening the opponent's face.
records.fullDescription: One of Meyer's inverted longsword cuts (Forgeng: 'Plummet Cut'). Although it is a form of Oberhau, it is named for the way it plummets headlong in the cut-through: as you cut from above you turn the point over and down so that at the end it is aimed at the opponent's face in the Ox guard. Meyer notes it differs only slightly from the Scheitelhau (Hairline/Scalp Cut). It is used mostly in the approach or onset (Zufechten), where dropping the point over the opponent's guard brings the point to bear even though Meyer's sportive longsword no longer delivers a true thrust.
records.briefApplication: Use the Sturzhau in the onset to plunge your point over the opponent's guard and menace their face from above.
records.fullApplication: A provoking cut for the Zufechten: by tipping the point down into Ochs you reach over the opponent's blade and threaten the face without committing to a full percussive cut, drawing a reaction you can exploit in the handwork. It flows naturally from the high guards and, once contact is made, sets up crossing cuts or winding. In a system where the thrust proper has been set aside, the Sturzhau preserves the value of a point-forward threat while remaining a cut.

records.briefDescription: A deceptive bind-work cut that 'blinds' the opponent by flicking the weak of the blade at the head on one side while the hilt works below on the other.
records.fullDescription: One of Meyer's inverted longsword cuts (Forgeng/Wiktenauer: 'Obscured Cut'); its name comes from blenden, to blind or dazzle. Bind onto the opponent's sword from your right. In the bind, wind through below toward their left side with the hilt or grip; when they chase the winding, quickly flick the weak (the front end) of the blade from your right toward their left at the head with crossed hands, then wind back through or rip out to your left with the half edge. Meyer notes it is executed in many ways.
records.briefApplication: Use the Blendhau in the bind to draw the opponent's blade and attention one way, then flick to the head on the other.
records.fullApplication: A handwork deception: the hilt-work below 'shows' one threat so the opponent commits to chasing it, opening the head for the flicking weak coming from the far side. Use it when bound at the sword and the opponent is following your winding—mislead their defense with the low action, then snap the point-end in to the exposed opening before they can re-cover.

records.briefDescription: An inverted high cut that glances off the opponent's blade with the flat so the short edge sweeps over the hands onto the head.
records.fullDescription: One of Meyer's inverted (verkehrt) longsword cuts. When the opponent cuts from above, strike with reversed or inverted hands against their strike at the upper left opening; let your blade glance off theirs with the reversed flat sliding down it, so that the short edge, carried by the sweep, travels over their hands and strikes the head. It uses the opponent's own blade as a rail to redirect your short edge onto the opening rather than opposing strength to strength.
records.briefApplication: Use the Glancing Cut to answer a high cut by sliding off the opponent's blade with the flat and landing the short edge on the head over the hands.
records.fullApplication: A counter to an Oberhau that turns the opponent's blade to your advantage: instead of meeting force with force you let the blades glance so your short edge continues over the hands to the head. Use it when the opponent cuts high and you can meet with inverted hands, converting their attack into your opening in a single deflecting motion.

records.briefDescription: A rising answer that catches a descending strike on the raised crossguard, then drives the pommel up to strike the head with the half edge behind the opponent's blade.
records.fullDescription: One of Meyer's inverted longsword cuts, named for the 'crown' formed by the raised hilt over the head. From Pflug, or otherwise fencing up from a low stance, when the opponent cuts from above, raise the crossguard horizontally and catch their strike in the air on your ricasso (schilt) or crossguard; as soon as it glances off, quickly thrust the pommel upward and strike them with the half edge behind their blade on the head. The raised hilt both crowns and covers your head while you answer.
records.briefApplication: Use the Crown Cut to catch a strong descending cut on your raised hilt and immediately answer to the head with the half edge.
records.fullApplication: A defensive-offensive answer to a powerful Oberhau when you are working up from below, where a simple rising cut would be overpowered: the raised crossguard traps their blade and shields your head, and the pommel-driven half-edge blow reaches over their sword to the head in one continuous motion. Use it against committed high cuts, catching in the air and answering before they can recover the line.

records.briefDescription: A changing cut that flows from side to side and from high to low in front of the opponent to mislead them.
records.fullDescription: One of Meyer's inverted longsword cuts. As Meyer puts it, the Change Cut is nothing more than changing, with cuts, from one side to the other and from above to below and back again, in front of the opponent in order to confuse them. Rather than a single fixed blow it is a manner of flowing, feinting cutwork that continually shifts line and height so the opponent cannot fix on your intention, from which you then strike the true opening once they are misled.
records.briefApplication: Use the Wechselhau to flow cuts from side to side and high to low, unsettling the opponent before striking the real opening.
records.fullApplication: A provoking, deceptive device for the approach and onset: by continually changing the side and height of your cuts you deny the opponent a settled read and bait either a reaction or a committed parry, then cut to the opening their change of guard exposes. It embodies Meyer's emphasis on flowing, misleading cutwork over single committed blows, and pairs naturally with changing through (Durchwechseln) when the opponent tries to bind.

records.briefDescription: A concealed short-edge cut that feigns a Krumphau bind, then passes under the opponent's blade to strike the head with crossed arms.
records.fullDescription: One of Meyer's inverted longsword cuts, which he calls a 'secret passage-through.' When the opponent cuts from above, position yourself as if you wanted to bind on their sword with a Krumphau (that is, with the short edge), but do not; instead pass beneath their sword, moving quickly through underneath, and strike with the short edge and crossed arms over their right arm at the head—so that you catch their sword with your long edge as you land. It is named 'short' because it strikes with the short (half) edge on a concealed, abbreviated path.
records.briefApplication: Use the Short Cut to feint a Krumphau bind, slip under the opponent's blade, and strike the head with the short edge.
records.fullApplication: A deceptive counter to a high cut that steals the tempo: the threatened Krump draws the opponent to expect a bind, and by declining it and passing under their sword you arrive at the head from an unexpected line while catching their blade with your long edge for cover. Use it when the opponent commits an Oberhau and you can go under rather than oppose, converting their attack into an opening at the head.

records.briefDescription: The act of rotating your blade against or around your opponent's sword in the bind while keeping your point oriented toward their openings, creating leverage and new angles of attack.
records.fullDescription:
Once your blade is in contact with your opponent's (in the bind), rotate your sword by turning your hands and arms while maintaining blade contact. The motion is circular—you're winding around the opponent's blade rather than pulling away or pushing straight through. There are two types of winding relative to the opponent's blade: Inner winding (turning your hilt toward their blade, creating a convex pressing angle) and outer winding (turning your hilt away from their blade, allowing your point to cross behind theirs).

The four hengen (hangings)—right and left Ochs, right and left Pflug—are the endpoint positions of winding actions. As you wind, your point should always remain forward and threatening, creating a somewhat circular path rather than removing threat. The strong part of your blade should work toward controlling the weak part of theirs. Your hands and body work together—small rotations of the wrists combined with larger rotations of the forearms and shoulders. Your feet may need to adjust to maintain proper structure and pressure. The key is maintaining contact throughout—you're not disengaging but rather rotating around the point of contact.
records.fullApplication:
Use winding as your primary means of continuing an attack once you have established a bind, working in the Mittel (middle) where Meyer places the Handarbeit (handwork). Winding excels at transforming defensive situations into offensive ones—after you catch or meet your opponent's attack, immediately wind to bring your point back online toward their openings while keeping the safety of blade contact.

Based on what you feel (fühlen) in the bind—whether they are hard (strong) or soft (weak)—you choose which wind and which target. If they are soft, wind so your point sinks over their blade to thrust low (the idea behind Mutieren). If they are hard, turn to the short edge to strike or work around their blade (as in Verkehren and Duplieren) rather than fighting their strength. If they are equal, wind your strong against their weak to leverage the bind.

Use winding whenever you are at the sword and need to attack a different opening than your current line addresses. Meyer stresses staying firm on the bind (am Band bleiben) as you wind, so that defense (contact) and offense (threat) are maintained together. From a winding position you can deliver any of the three: cut, thrust, or slice.

Winding is one of the central and most sophisticated parts of the art, marking the transition from the fencer who merely strikes in the onset to one who works skillfully at the sword. Practice turning smoothly between the hanging positions to either side, keeping your point forward and threatening throughout.
records.briefApplication: Use winding as your primary method of continuing your attack after you've established a bind.

records.briefDescription: The act of establishing and maintaining blade contact with your opponent's sword, creating a connection through which you can feel their pressure, control the line, and transition to offensive actions.
records.fullDescription:
Create blade-to-blade contact by intercepting, meeting, or seeking your opponent's sword with your own. The bind should involve firm but not excessive pressure—enough contact to maintain connection and gather information, but not so much that you're rigidly locked. Your blade should contact theirs at a point where you have structural advantage—ideally your strong (forte, near the hilt) against their weak (foible, near the point).

The bind creates a single point of connection between the two swords that becomes the fulcrum for all subsequent actions. Your hands, arms, and body should maintain structure through the bind—don't collapse or over-extend. The bind should feel alive and responsive rather than static. You should be actively feeling (fühlen) through the connection, gathering information about your opponent's pressure, intentions, and reactions.

The bind can occur at different heights (high, middle, low) and on different sides (inside, outside) of your body. Your feet and body position should support the bind, allowing you to maintain or increase pressure as needed.
records.fullApplication:
Use binding as the gateway to Meyer's Mittel (middle), the close phase where the Handarbeit (handwork) is done. Once you have established a bind through your initial strike or interception, you pass from the Zufechten (onset) into the middle, where winding, feeling, and skilled blade work dominate. The bind lets you control your opponent's sword while threatening them—as long as you keep contact they cannot simply pull back and strike freely, and you gather information about their state (hard/soft, strong/weak).

Use binding to 'test' your opponent: form a bind, feel how they respond, then immediately exploit their reaction with the appropriate technique. If they push hard, do not meet strength with strength—yield and turn to the short edge, or leave with Zucken or Durchwechseln. If they are soft, press through with winding or a thrust. The bind is where you apply feeling (fühlen) and act in the instant (Indes).

Form binds deliberately when you want to work at close measure, and hold them while they give you advantage. Meyer treats the bind as the doorway to his handwork, where openings and opportunities are discovered.

Don't fear the bind; it is the arena where skilled fencers distinguish themselves from beginners who only strike. Practice keeping proper pressure in the bind—not so hard you are committed and rigid, not so soft you lose contact and control.
records.briefApplication: Use binding as the gateway to the Mittel (middle), where Meyer's handwork (Handarbeit) is done.

records.briefDescription: A defensive handwork that wards an incoming cut or thrust and in the same motion counters, setting the opponent's weapon aside with your edge while your point threatens them.
records.fullDescription:
As your opponent attacks with a cut or thrust, extend your arms forward and set their blade aside with your long (true) edge while simultaneously aiming your point at their face, throat, or chest. The motion is a unified ward-and-counter: you are not blocking first then countering, but setting off their weapon in a way that naturally deflects it while your point arrives on target. Against an Oberhau you go up with the long edge into a hanging so their stroke is caught and carried off; against a thrust you turn your hilt up and set their point aside with the outside flat or edge while your forward point stays out toward them.

Your hands extend forward and up or to the side as needed, keeping your point toward the opponent's opening. Step out (Austritt) as you set off, to add body commitment behind your counter. Your blade should meet theirs strong against weak for leverage. Meyer defines this handwork as the right way of warding (abtragen/versetzen): you receive the strike and, in the same moment the setting-off touches, strike or thrust to their opening with the step. The key is simultaneity—defense and offense are one action, not two.
records.fullApplication:
Use Absetzen as your primary defensive counter whenever you respond to an attack in the Nach (after). It transforms defense into immediate offense—instead of purely blocking, you defend by threatening. Absetzen works against both cuts and thrusts, which makes it versatile.

Against a descending strike (Oberhau), go up with the long edge into a hanging to catch and carry their stroke off while your point threatens their face or chest. Against a thrust (from Ochs or Pflug), turn your hilt up and set their point aside with the outside flat or edge while your forward point stays out toward them. Practice setting off from both sides—right and left—stepping out as you counter.

The technique is most effective when you meet their attack early, before it develops full speed and commitment. Absetzen embodies Meyer's principle of good warding: you do not merely receive the blow, you answer it in the same tempo. Afterward you stand with their weapon set aside and your point threatening, well placed to press, wind if they bind, or strike around if they pull away.

Practice it thoroughly as a core idea of the handwork: there is no purely passive defense here, only warding that simultaneously creates offense.
records.briefApplication: Use Absetzen (setting off) as your primary defensive counter whenever you respond to an attack in the Nach, warding the cut or thrust while your point threatens in the same tempo.

records.briefDescription: A technique of disengaging your point by dropping it under (or around) your opponent's blade to thrust to the opposite opening while remaining in measure.
records.fullDescription:
When your blade is in contact with or approaching your opponent's blade, quickly dip your point downward and pass it underneath (or around) their sword, then immediately extend to thrust on the opposite side. The motion should be quick and minimal—don't make large, sweeping movements but rather a tight, efficient loop under their blade. Your hands stay relatively in place while your point describes a small arc under their sword's edge.

As your point clears their blade on the underside, immediately extend to thrust at the newly opened target. Your body should step forward slightly as you complete the thrust. The technique works from either side—you can drop under and change from right to left or left to right. Keep your hands high enough during the exchange that you maintain defensive structure. The motion is analogous to a cavazione in rapier fencing—a quick disengage under the blade. The key is speed and efficiency: if you're slow or use large motions, your opponent can follow and strike you as you disengage.
records.fullApplication:
Use Durchwechseln when your opponent binds onto your sword (especially if they have leverage advantage) or when they attempt to displace or parry your initial thrust. This technique excels at solving the problem of blade obstruction—if your line is blocked, simply go around to the open side. The sources specify that Durchwechseln 'surely finds those who bind onto you,' meaning it works well against opponents who commit heavily to controlling your blade.

When you thrust from Pflug or Ochs and your opponent moves to intercept or displace, don't fight their blade—instead, Durchwechsel under and thrust to the opposite side where they're now open. Use this technique in Zufechten (approach phase) when your initial thrust is intercepted but you're not yet fully in the bind. If you Durchwechsel from your right side, thrust to their left side; if from your left, thrust to their right.

The technique can also work as a feint—threaten one side to draw their parry, then change through to the open side. Practice smooth, quick execution: the point dips just enough to clear their blade, then immediately extends to target. Don't make it a two-tempo action (disengage THEN thrust) but rather one flowing motion (disengage-to-thrust).

Durchwechseln is particularly effective when your opponent is aggressive about controlling blades but not quick enough to follow your point through the change. Be careful not to telegraph—if you pull back or make large preparatory motions, skilled opponents will strike your opening immediately.
records.briefApplication: Use Durchwechseln when your opponent binds onto your sword (especially if they have leverage advantage) or when they attempt to displace or parry your initial thrust.

records.briefDescription: A technique of lifting your blade completely off and away from the bind, then striking around to the opposite opening while your opponent's committed parry leaves them open.
records.fullDescription:
From a bind, lift your sword up off contact with your opponent's blade and immediately strike around to the other side—the action Meyer names striking around (Umbschlagen) or snapping around (Umbschnappen). Unlike Zucken (a deceptive twitch that finishes back at the same opening) or Durchwechseln (which passes under the blade), taking-off lifts your blade over or away from the bind and delivers a fresh strike to the opening their parry has left. The motion typically raises your hands and blade, then cuts back down or across to the opposite opening, often letting it snap in with the short edge.

Your body stays engaged and forward—you are not retreating, only removing your blade to strike elsewhere. It is best used when the opponent has parried strongly to one side, opening the other. After you lift off, strike quickly before they can recover their position.
records.fullApplication:
Use taking-off (striking around) when your opponent commits strongly to a parry in the bind, driving your blade to one side and exposing the other. It exploits overcommitted defenses—when someone wards so hard that their structure goes offline, you lift off their pressure and strike the exposed opposite opening.

Read the moment: their hands and blade are committed to one side, their body follows, and the far opening becomes available. Lift your blade clear and strike around quickly and decisively, letting it snap in; any delay lets them recover. Where Meyer's Duplieren doubles a single cut on the spot (long edge, then short edge behind their blade), striking around leaves the bind entirely to hit a different opening.

This teaches the principle of not fighting strong pressure but avoiding it and striking where there is no resistance. Combine it freely with the other handworks—following a strong bind, an over-hard parry, or a failed strike—to keep the initiative and flow from one opening to the next.
records.briefApplication: Use Abnehmen when your opponent commits heavily to a parry in the bind, pushing your blade strongly to one side and creating an opening on the other side.

records.briefDescription: A deceptive twitch in the bind: after binding or cutting in at one opening with the long edge, you jerk your blade up as if to strike the other side, then finish with the short edge back at the same opening to beat the opponent's parry.
records.fullDescription:
After you have bound on or cut in at an opening with your long edge, twitch (zuck) your blade briskly back up as though you meant to strike to the other side. Do not carry that strike through—instead, as your opponent moves to parry the side you feigned, quickly complete the cut with the short (half) edge back at the very opening you departed from. The pull is small and sharp, giving the action a snapping, on-off quality rather than a smooth withdrawal.

Your hands make a short backward loop up before driving the short-edge cut back in. The timing is critical: the feint and the finish must happen faster than your opponent can commit to and recover from the parry you drew. Your body stays engaged throughout—you are not stepping back, only pulling the blade to mislead. Meyer counts pulling among the very good handworks precisely because it masterfully deceives (verführt) a defender into warding a strike that never lands where they expect.
records.fullApplication:
Use Zucken as a deception once you are at the sword: feign a strike to the far side to draw your opponent's parry, then finish with the short edge back at the opening you first threatened (or wherever they have now uncovered). Meyer calls pulling a very good handwork for masterfully misleading (verführen) your counterpart.

Bind or cut in to an opening with the long edge, twitch up as if going to the other side, and as they chase your feigned strike, snap the short-edge cut back in. Because the pull and finish come so fast, they cannot follow your blade. You can pull from any bind and to either side; the essence is the on-off, twitching quality that confuses the defender.

Combine Zucken with footwork—pull while stepping slightly out or around, then drive the finishing cut in. Practice the timing until the feint and the completed short-edge strike feel like one continuous action rather than two tempos. Used well, pulling lets you strike an opponent who has committed to parrying the wrong line.
records.briefApplication: Use Zucken to deceive: feint a strike to the other side, then finish with the short edge back at the opening you first threatened.

records.briefDescription: A doubling of the cut: after your first cut is caught in the bind, you thrust the pommel through under your arm and strike again behind the opponent's blade with the short edge, so one cut is delivered twice—first long edge, then short.
records.fullDescription:
Cut first from your right to your opponent's ear (or other opening) with the long edge. As the swords clash together in the bind, thrust your sword's pommel through under your right arm and drive upward with both arms at once, bringing your blade over so that you strike with the short (half) edge behind their blade onto their head. Because the same cut is thereby completed twice—first with the long edge, then with the short—Meyer names this handwork Doubling.

The action stays close and immediate: you do not wind slowly or leave the bind, but let the clash itself set up the second, short-edge strike behind their blade. Your crossed hands and raised arms carry your point and edge over their steel to the head, striking around their parry without a full new wind-up. Keep your body forward and committed so the doubled cut lands before they can adjust to the sudden reversal of your edge.
records.fullApplication:
Use Duplieren immediately when your first cut is caught or parried in the bind, especially against a firm parry to your strong side. Rather than pulling back to wind up a new blow, you double the cut on the spot: as the blades clash, pommel through under your arm and strike the short edge behind their blade to the head.

The technique is most reliable when they meet your cut strongly, because their commitment to the parry holds their blade in place while your short edge comes around behind it. Practice the sequence from a cut to the ear—long-edge cut, clash, pommel-through, short-edge strike behind the blade—until the second strike flows out of the first without a pause.

Meyer's reproduced verse pairs 'double above' with 'mutate below,' but his own handwork defines Doubling concretely as this twofold cut (long edge, then short) rather than as a felt hard/soft choice. Use it whenever a caught cut leaves the opening still reachable behind your opponent's own blade, keeping your point and edge working close to their steel throughout.
records.briefApplication: Use Duplieren to double a caught cut: as the blades clash, strike again with the short edge behind your opponent's blade to the head.

records.briefDescription: A transformation of the thrust in the bind: you raise your hilt and let your point sink down over the opponent's blade to thrust to their lower opening—turning a high bind into a low thrust (and the low into a high).
records.fullDescription:
From an upper bind or thrust, raise your hands so that your hilt goes high and your blade turns over the top of your opponent's blade; then let your point sink down over their steel and drive a thrust to their lower openings (belly, hips, groin). By lifting the hilt and dropping the point over their blade, you transform (mutate) a high engagement into a low thrust—for example turning a right Ox into a right Plow and thrusting from below to their hilt or hand. The same principle runs the other way: a low thrust can be turned into a high one by heaving the hilt and coming over the arm.

Your raised hilt and crossed structure help keep their blade down and offline as your point comes over it, so the low thrust is hard to intercept. Drive your body forward behind the thrust. Meyer treats this as transforming the nature of the attack—an upper cut or bind mutates into a thrust beneath the opponent's blade.
records.fullApplication:
Use Mutieren to change the height of your attack in the bind: when your high thrust or bind is warded, raise your hilt, roll your point over their blade, and thrust to a lower opening—and reverse it (low into high) if they cover below. It excels at reaching openings behind a defender's blade, because your point comes over their steel from above while your hilt keeps their weapon down.

When you thrust or bind high and they move to close that line, don't fight it—heave the hilt and let the point sink over into a low thrust to the belly, hip, or groin; if they then guard low, come back over the arm to the face. This transforming of high into low (and low into high) is the essence of mutating.

Meyer's reproduced verse pairs 'mutate below' with 'double above,' but in his own practice Mutieren appears chiefly in the thrust-work rather than as a felt soft/hard response. Practice rolling smoothly from a high bind into the low thrust and back, keeping your point over the opponent's blade so it stays controlled as you change lines.
records.briefApplication: Use Mutieren to transform a warded high thrust or bind into a low thrust, rolling your point over the opponent's blade to reach beneath it (and reverse it, low into high).

records.briefDescription: A slicing action in which you catch the opponent's incoming cuts on your long edge and slice them off to either side, controlling their blade until you find an opening for further work.
records.fullDescription:
Hold your sword with outstretched arms long in front of you, or sink into the guard Alber (Fool). When your opponent cuts long strokes at you, receive and slice them off with your long edge to both sides—meeting each stroke and carrying it away rather than blocking dead—continuing as long and as often as needed until you see your advantage to pass to other, more suitable work.

The motion is a drawing slice along the edge, not a percussive parry: you catch their blade and let your edge cut and guide it off line. Because you keep contact and slice rather than merely stopping the blow, you stay connected to their weapon and can flow directly into the bind, a thrust, or a slice to their arms. From this same slicing you can turn your long edge onto their hands or forearms when they overreach, but the core of Abschneiden is slicing their strokes off from you to both sides.
records.fullApplication:
Use Abschneiden when your opponent throws long strokes at you and you want to control them safely rather than trade blows. Standing long before you, or in Alber, catch each incoming cut on your long edge and slice it off to the side; slice off both right and left as their attacks come, staying calm and connected until an opening or advantage appears.

Because you slice off rather than block, you remain on their blade and can immediately follow into a thrust, a bind, or a slice to their arms. This is close, controlling work: when full strikes are risky, slicing their attacks off keeps you safe while you look for the moment to seize the initiative. Meyer notes that chasing (Nachreisen) and the slice are bound up with this slicing off.

Use it especially against an opponent who cuts in repeatedly and long, exposing their blade and hands as they overcommit. Slice their strokes off, and when they overreach, turn your long edge onto their hands or forearms, or pass into the nearest opening. The lesson is economy and control—you do not always need a full counter-cut; a well-placed slicing-off both defends and sets up your attack.
records.briefApplication: Use Abschneiden to slice the opponent's long strokes off with your long edge to both sides, controlling their blade until an opening appears.

records.briefDescription: A handwork in which, from the bind, you reverse your hand and let your blade run off downward with the short edge while pulling your hilt up into a fresh strike—done to either side.
records.fullDescription:
From a bind on either side, as the blades clash, turn (reverse) your hand and let your blade run off downward along the short (half) edge, so it slips off your opponent's blade instead of pressing or fighting for the bind. In the same motion, pull (zuck) your hilt up high into a new strike. The blade 'runs off' downward and around while your hilt rises, so that leaving the bind and loading the next blow are one continuous action. This can be done from both sides.

The motion is smooth and flowing rather than a hard shove or a dead disengage: your blade sinks and runs off their steel while your hands rotate the hilt upward. As your blade clears theirs, you are already gathering the strike from above. Keep your body engaged and let footwork support the new line.
records.fullApplication:
Use Ablauffen when a bind offers you nothing to push against—or when meeting your opponent's strength directly is a poor bargain—so instead of fighting for the bind you let your blade run off downward and pull your hilt up to strike anew. Rather than staying to wrestle in the bind, you flow off their blade and reload a stroke from above in the same tempo.

This is standard handwork in Meyer's middle, not a last resort: it is a way to leave a bind that has stalled and immediately threaten again from a fresh angle, keeping the initiative.
