Practice distance judgment: know exactly when you're in range and launch your Zufechten strike at that moment, not too early (falling short) or too late (giving them time to preempt). Remember that Zufechten is not just about physical approach but about tactical approach: you're setting up the entire exchange through your guard choice, approach path, and opening strike. Make deliberate tactical choices during Zufechten that give you advantages in the subsequent Handarbeit phase. If your opening strike doesn't hit (because they defended), transition immediately to Handarbeit by working in the bind they've created—don't pull back or pause. The phases should flow: Zufechten leads directly into Handarbeit when they defend, or into Abzug if you hit or need to disengage. Master Zufechten and you enter every exchange with purpose, structure, and tactical advantage, setting up favorable situations for the close work to follow.
records.definition: The approach/opening phase before handwork.
records.briefDescription: The approach/opening phase before handwork.
records.fullDescription: Zufechten (onset, approaching, pre-fencing) is the first phase of combat where you approach your opponent and initiate engagement, beginning from the moment you start moving toward each other until you establish blade contact or close to binding range. This phase is particularly emphasized in Joachim Meyer's 1570 system as the first of three distinct phases (Zufechten, then das Mittel or Handarbeit—the Middle/Handwork, then Abzug), though the concept exists in earlier Liechtenauer tradition as well. During Zufechten, you: close distance from long range to fighting range; launch opening strikes from your guards (Leger/Huten); attempt to win the Vorschlag (first strike); establish initial control or provoke reactions; assess your opponent's intentions and guard choices. Execute Zufechten by beginning in one of the primary guards (typically Vom Tag, Ochs, Pflug, or Alber), then as you enter measure, strike with committed cuts or thrusts to your opponent's openings. These opening strikes should be powerful and genuine threats, forcing your opponent to respond. The Zufechten strike typically aims to either hit directly (if your opponent is passive or poorly positioned), or to establish a favorable bind (if they defend). Your footwork during Zufechten should close distance while maintaining structure and balance—typically using deliberate, measured steps or occasionally more explosive entries. The five Meisterhäue (master strikes) are particularly associated with Zufechten, as they are long-range attacks from the approach phase. The Zufechten ends when you establish blade contact (beginning das Mittel/Handarbeit) or when the exchange completes and you disengage (beginning Abzug).
records.briefApplication: Use the concept of Zufechten to frame your tactical approach during the initial phase of combat—from the moment you're at distance until you establish close engagement.

records.fullApplication: Use the concept of Handarbeit to frame your approach to close-range combat with blade contact, emphasizing sophisticated technique over raw force. This phase excels at rewarding technical skill, tactical sensitivity, and rapid decision-making over physical attributes. Once you establish blade contact (from Zufechten or from any strike that's parried), immediately enter Handarbeit mindset: stay engaged with their blade, feel their pressure, and work continuously based on what you perceive. The goals during Handarbeit are: (1) Maintain blade contact when tactically advantageous—don't leave the bind unnecessarily, as contact gives you control and information. (2) Feel (Fühlen) continuously to assess their pressure state—hard, soft, or neutral—then choose appropriate techniques. (3) Wind constantly to bring your point toward openings while maintaining the safety of blade contact. Your point should always threaten; winding lets you change which opening you're threatening without losing contact. (4) Execute appropriate techniques based on pressure and situation: if hard, use yielding techniques (Zucken, Durchwechseln); if soft, use pressing techniques (winding to thrust, Mutieren). (5) Work rapidly and continuously—don't pause or think slowly. Handarbeit requires speed and fluidity: feel → decide → act, all nearly instantaneous. (6) Attack from one opening to another—if they defend one line, immediately work to the next opening. Keep them constantly defending. Practice Handarbeit extensively through bind-focused drilling: establish blade contact with training partners and practice all the binding/winding techniques with emphasis on feeling pressure and responding appropriately. This phase is where most of the system's technique catalog lives: winding, Duplieren, Mutieren, Zucken, Durchwechseln, Abschneiden (slicing), various wrestling applications, and more. Each technique is a tool for specific Handarbeit situations. Develop automatic responses: feel hard → execute yielding technique; feel soft → execute pressing technique. This should become instinctive through practice. Handarbeit also includes transitioning to wrestling (Ringen am Schwert) when appropriate: if you're in very close range with blade contact and opportunity arises, transition to grappling techniques, throws, disarms, or pommel strikes. Meyer emphasizes that Handarbeit 'comprises the greatest art'—this is where technical mastery matters most. Physical strength matters less in skilled Handarbeit because you're using leverage, timing, and technique rather than force. Practice continuous flow: establish bind, feel, wind, thrust/cut/slice based on opening and pressure, and if that's defended, immediately continue to next action. Never stop working in Handarbeit—maintain constant pressure and activity. The phase tests your ability to gather information through touch (Fühlen), make rapid tactical decisions, and execute techniques precisely under pressure. Remember that Handarbeit is not about desperately struggling in the bind but about skillful, efficient work that exploits every opportunity. Stay calm, feel constantly, make smart technique choices, and maintain offensive pressure throughout. Master Handarbeit and you become dangerous at close range where technical skill dominates, able to work efficiently in the bind to find and exploit openings that less skilled opponents cannot perceive or capitalize on. This is the heart of sophisticated longsword fencing.
records.definition: The in-fight phase where technique decides the exchange.
records.briefDescription: The in-fight phase where technique decides the exchange.
records.fullDescription: Handarbeit (handwork), which Meyer also names das Mittel (the Middle), is the second phase of combat where you work at close range with blade contact, executing sophisticated techniques based on feeling (Fühlen), winding, binding, and rapid tactical decisions. The winding-based exchange that unfolds within the bind—winding, slicing, wrenching out, and reversing—is what Meyer (following the Liechtenauer tradition) calls the Krieg (War). This is the phase that begins when blades make contact (after Zufechten) and continues until you hit your opponent or disengage. Meyer (1570) particularly emphasizes Handarbeit as the middle phase where 'the greatest art and all speed which can take place in fencing' occurs. During Handarbeit, you: maintain blade contact through binds; feel (fühlen) your opponent's pressure to assess whether they're hard or soft; wind to bring your point to new openings while maintaining contact; execute techniques like Duplieren, Mutieren, Zucken, Durchwechseln, Schneiden (slicing), and others based on what you feel; work rapidly from one opening to another based on your opponent's reactions; potentially transition to grappling (Ringen am Schwert) at very close range. Execute Handarbeit by staying actively engaged in the bind: don't passively hold blade contact, but constantly work—feeling pressure, winding to openings, choosing techniques based on hard/soft states, maintaining offensive threat through continuous action. Your hands and blade should be in constant subtle motion, adjusting, winding, seeking openings. The Handarbeit phase requires the highest technical skill because you must make rapid tactical decisions based on tactile information (Fühlen) while maintaining structure, balance, and offensive pressure. This is where the system's sophistication appears: beginners only know how to strike, but advanced practitioners excel in Handarbeit where technique, sensitivity, and tactical intelligence dominate.
records.briefApplication: Use the concept of Handarbeit to frame your approach to close-range combat with blade contact, emphasizing sophisticated technique over raw force.

records.briefDescription: The four target zones of the opponent—upper and lower, right and left—that all cuts and thrusts should attack.
records.fullDescription: The Vier Blößen (four openings) are the four target areas into which Meyer divides the opponent, and they form the targeting framework beneath the whole system. A vertical line splits the opponent into right and left, and a horizontal line splits him into upper and lower, giving four quarters: upper right, upper left, lower right, lower left. Meyer teaches that the two upper openings belong to the Ox (Ochs) and the two lower openings to the Plow (Pflug), and that all of your cuts and thrusts should be directed at or toward these four parts. In his dedicated chapter on the four openings (chapter 10, 'How one should fence at the four openings'), Meyer stresses that everything you do should be aimed at one of the four, and that you must likewise keep your own four openings guarded against the opponent. The four openings organize both attack and defense: you strike to whichever quarter is exposed, and when the opponent moves to cover it, he necessarily uncovers another, to which you then go.
records.briefApplication: Direct every cut and thrust at one of the four openings, and when it is covered, immediately attack the opening the defense uncovers.
records.fullApplication: Use the Vier Blößen as the aiming framework for all of your work, in the Onset and in the handwork alike. Rather than striking vaguely, target a specific opening; when the opponent moves to cover that quarter, he must expose another, so redirect your attack to the newly opened one. Meyer's rhymed teaching captures the pattern: 'break the four openings' with skill, 'double above' (double your attack to an upper opening, e.g. with Duplieren), and 'transmute below' (mutate the work down to a lower opening—for example the arms—with Mutieren). Provoke a defense at one opening to draw a reaction, then strike to the opening it uncovers, keeping the opponent perpetually defending while you flow from target to target. Defensively, keep your own four openings covered—the two upper with Ochs-type coverage, the two lower with Pflug-type coverage—so that you are not the one who is opened. Drill by having a partner present and cover openings while you learn to feel which quarter is exposed and set your cut or thrust onto it at once.

records.briefDescription: The winding exchange in the bind, where each fencer answers the other's actions blade-to-blade.
records.fullDescription: The Krieg (War) is Meyer's term for the close winding-work that unfolds once the blades are bound. Meyer names it directly: winding, slicing, wrenching out, and reversing in the bind 'is called the War, through which one to the other always counters the opponent's techniques.' In the Krieg the two fencers remain on the sword and exchange counters back and forth—if one wards off a technique, that very act opens the way to the next, so the work chains from one action to another ('thus you both make War'). The Krieg is not a separate phase but the core of the Middle/Handwork (das Mittel / Handarbeit): after you bind—for instance when the opponent binds Crooked on your sword—you do not pull away at once, but remain, feel (Fühlen) what work is needed, and carry out the Krieg with winding and the related handwork. It is governed by Indes and Fühlen: you feel the opponent's pressure and, in the instant, choose the winding, slice, or reversal that answers it.
records.briefApplication: When you bind, remain on the sword, feel the pressure, and work winding, slicing, and reversing back and forth until an opening appears.
records.fullApplication: Enter the Krieg whenever a bind forms, rather than immediately breaking away. Meyer's instruction against a Crooked bind is representative: 'remain rightly on the sword, carry out the Krieg with winding, slicing, and what's more.' Stay on the blade, feel (Fühlen) whether the opponent is hard or soft, and answer Indes—wind to a new opening, slice, wrench out, or reverse; when the opponent counters that, let his reaction open the next line so your work follows one action from another. The Krieg rewards sensitivity and continuous work over force: because each counter creates the occasion for the next technique, the fencer who feels and acts in the instant keeps control of the bind. Do not overextend or fly wildly from opening to opening—Meyer warns that once you leave the bind carelessly you surrender its control; instead remain, work the War methodically, and break off only when you have found your opening or must withdraw. Tie the Krieg to the four openings: each winding and reversal should be aimed at an exposed quarter, converting the pressure you feel into an attack on whichever opening the opponent leaves.

Use the concept of Abzug to frame your approach to safe disengagement and withdrawal after exchanges have concluded. This phase excels at ensuring you don't get hit during retreat, teaching the tactical principle that leaving the fight safely is as important as entering it or fighting in it. After you've completed an exchange—whether you've hit your opponent, they've defended successfully, or the exchange has become inconclusive—initiate Abzug by withdrawing while maintaining defensive structure. The goals during Abzug are: (1) Disengage safely from blade contact without leaving yourself open to counters or pursuing attacks. (2) Retreat from fighting range back to safe distance while maintaining structure. Don't turn your back or drop your guard. (3) Protect against afterblows—your opponent may attempt to strike you as you withdraw, so maintain defensive capability throughout. (4) Return to a ready guard position, typically Pflug or another stance that covers you during withdrawal. Execute Abzug by cutting as you step backward: as you withdraw, cut in the direction you're moving (typically cutting down and back), creating a barrier with your sword that protects you during retreat. Your footwork should be controlled—step backward smoothly while maintaining balance, don't stumble or rush. Some instructors recommend specific withdrawal techniques: cut toward your opponent as you step back to maintain threat and coverage; recover to Pflug because it keeps your hands low and safe while your point still threatens forward (making it difficult for opponents to slash your arms during withdrawal); or use other cuts that create barriers as you retreat. Practice Abzug by drilling: complete an exchange (strike, bind, finish), then practice withdrawing safely with proper cutting and footwork. This should become automatic—after every exchange in practice, execute a proper Abzug rather than simply dropping your guard or turning away. The concept teaches important tactical awareness: every action has three parts (approaching/entering, working, leaving), and neglecting the third part leaves you vulnerable. In training contexts, good Abzug allows you to reset safely for the next exchange. In competitive contexts, it prevents afterblows and demonstrates control. In hypothetical real contexts, it ensures you don't get hit after landing your attack, as historical sources note that many fighters were injured during or after their own successful attacks. Meyer emphasizes Abzug as completing the tactical cycle: you enter deliberately (Zufechten), work skillfully (Handarbeit), and leave safely (Abzug). Master all three phases for complete tactical competence. Practice Abzug consciousness: in all training, don't just think about entering and hitting, but also think about leaving safely afterward. Make safe withdrawal habitual. Some variations of Abzug include not just cutting away but using other defensive actions: maintaining blade contact and pressing them backward as you retreat; executing specific techniques like Hendedrucken (pressing their hands/arms painfully to force them back); or transitioning through specific guard sequences that provide coverage during withdrawal. The key principle is that withdrawal should be active and defensive, not passive. Don't just retreat—cut, cover, maintain structure, and ensure you're not exposed to counters during your departure. Remember that the fight isn't over until you've safely disengaged, so treat Abzug with the same tactical attention as the other phases. Master Abzug and you complete your technical toolkit, ensuring you can enter safely, work skillfully, and leave safely—the full cycle of competent fencing.
records.definition: Exit phase to leave without being hit.
records.briefDescription: Exit phase to leave without being hit.
records.fullDescription: Abzug (withdrawal, departing, pulling away) is the third and final phase of combat where you safely disengage from your opponent after an exchange, retreating from fighting range without being hit. Meyer (1570) particularly emphasizes Abzug as the third phase of his three-part combat model (Zufechten, Handarbeit, Abzug), though the concept of safe withdrawal exists throughout the longsword tradition. During Abzug, you: disengage from blade contact safely; retreat from fighting range while maintaining defensive structure; protect yourself against potential afterblows or pursuing attacks; return to a guard position that covers you during withdrawal. Execute Abzug by cutting away as you withdraw—don't simply pull back or turn away, but cut as you step back, creating a barrier that protects you during retreat. The cut-and-withdraw motion should be coordinated: as your feet move backward, your sword cuts to maintain a defensive barrier. You can withdraw to various guards: Pflug is often recommended as safest because your hands are low and protected while your point still threatens; Ochs can also work but leaves your hands more exposed. Your withdrawal should be deliberate and controlled, not panicked or rushed. You're creating space while maintaining structure and defensive capability. The Abzug acknowledges a practical reality: not every exchange ends with your opponent disabled, and you need to be able to leave the engagement safely. This is particularly important in practice/training contexts where you want to reset for another exchange, but it's equally important in real contexts where withdrawing safely after landing a hit (or after an inconclusive exchange) is crucial to avoid afterblows.
records.briefApplication: Use the concept of Abzug to frame your approach to safe disengagement and withdrawal after exchanges have concluded.

records.fullApplication: Use Ringen am Schwert when you've closed to very close range where traditional sword techniques no longer work effectively, integrating wrestling skills with your sword to control, throw, disarm, or strike your opponent. This phase excels at ending fights decisively through grappling techniques enhanced by the sword as a leverage tool. The techniques apply when: (1) You've deliberately closed range through Durchlaufen (running through) and are now inside their reach. (2) In Handarbeit (close work), you've closed even tighter and have opportunity for wrestling. (3) Your opponent attempts to close on you and you need grappling responses. (4) The fight has naturally moved to very close range through the flow of exchange. Execute Ringen am Schwert by smoothly transitioning from sword technique to wrestling technique: maintain contact with their sword or body, then immediately apply grappling techniques that use your sword as enhancement. Common applications include: Throws using your sword as lever—place your blade against their neck, under their arm, or across their body, then use it as a rigid lever to throw them by pulling, pushing, or torquing. Trip them while using sword pressure to break their balance. Disarms (Schwertnehmen)—grab their blade or hilt, control their weapon with leverage, and strip it away or force them to release it. This often involves trapping their sword against your body or using two hands against their one. Pommel strikes—at very close range, release one hand from your sword and strike with your pommel to their head, face, or body. The heavy pommel makes an effective impact weapon at this range. Arm locks and controls—use your sword to trap or lever their arms, applying joint locks that force them to submit, drop their weapon, or move where you want. Wrestling throws and takedowns—apply standard wrestling techniques (hip throws, trips, takedowns) while using your sword for additional leverage, control, or off-balancing. Practice Ringen am Schwert with appropriate protective gear since these techniques involve close physical contact and potential falls. Train the transition from sword techniques to wrestling: practice moving smoothly from Handarbeit or Durchlaufen into wrestling applications. Develop your general wrestling skills as foundation—Ringen am Schwert requires competent grappling ability enhanced by the sword, not just sword technique. Study historical sources for specific techniques: many manuscripts show detailed Ringen am Schwert plays with specific throws, disarms, and strikes. Practice these historically-documented techniques to build your close-range toolkit. Remember that at very close range, your sword becomes a multipurpose tool: a lever for throws, a rigid bar for locks and controls, an impact weapon (pommel and crossguard), and a means to control their weapon. Use all these functions as situations demand. Ringen am Schwert teaches that longsword combat includes all ranges: from long cuts through middle binding to close wrestling—you must be competent at all ranges to be a complete fighter. Don't neglect this range in training. Practice deliberately closing to wrestling range, applying techniques, and transitioning back to sword range when appropriate. Master Ringen am Schwert and you become dangerous at all ranges, able to wrestle effectively even with swords in hand, using the weapon to enhance rather than limit your grappling options.
records.definition: Disarms, throws, pommel strikes once blades are engaged.
records.briefDescription: Disarms, throws, pommel strikes once blades are engaged.
records.fullDescription: Ringen am Schwert (wrestling at the sword, grappling with the sword) refers to all grappling, throwing, and close-combat techniques executed when swords are still in hand but fighters are at very close range. This represents the closest range of longsword combat, beyond the range where cutting and binding dominate. These techniques involve: throwing your opponent using your sword as a lever against their neck, arms, or body; disarming techniques (Schwertnehmen) where you strip away or control their sword; pommel strikes to the head, face, or body; arm locks and joint manipulations that disable or control; body-to-body wrestling that uses your sword for leverage while employing throws, trips, and takedowns. Execute Ringen am Schwert by first closing to very close range (often through Durchlaufen - running through), then immediately transitioning from sword techniques to wrestling techniques that incorporate the sword as a tool. Grip your sword at both hilt and blade to give yourself more control and leverage options—the sword becomes a rigid lever you can use against your opponent's body, neck, or arms. Common techniques include: placing your blade across their neck and using it as a lever to throw them backward; hooking their arms or neck with your blade and pulling/pushing to disrupt their balance; striking with your pommel to their head or face from close range; controlling their sword arm and using leverage to force them to release their weapon; various throws and takedowns that use your sword for additional leverage or control. Your wrestling skills become primary at this range—the sword enhances your grappling rather than replacing it.
records.briefApplication: This phase excels at ending fights decisively through grappling techniques enhanced by the sword as a leverage tool.

records.fullApplication: Use Schwertnehmen techniques when you're at very close range (typically during Ringen am Schwert) and opportunity arises to control and remove your opponent's weapon, ending the fight by disarming them. These techniques excel at decisive endings: without their weapon, your opponent is defeated (in training/competition) or at severe disadvantage (in historical context). Schwertnehmen opportunities typically arise when: (1) You've closed to wrestling range through Durchlaufen or close Handarbeit, bringing you within reach of their hilt or blade. (2) Their weapon is positioned where you can safely grab it—often when they've overextended, when it's bound or trapped, or when you've moved inside their guard. (3) You've controlled their arms or body in ways that limit their ability to withdraw or reorient their weapon. Execute Schwertnehmen by identifying the opportunity, immediately controlling their weapon with one hand (grabbing blade at flat, grabbing hilt, or hooking with your crossguard), then using leverage to strip it away. Common methods include: Two-hands-against-one: grab their hilt with one hand while maintaining your own weapon with your other hand, using your mechanical advantage to twist or pull their sword from their grip. Lever-strip: trap their blade against your body or with your sword, then use your free hand to grab and twist their hilt, levering the weapon from their hands. Joint-lock disarm: apply wrist or arm lock that forces them to release their weapon to avoid injury. Crossguard-hook: use your crossguard to hook their blade, then twist and pull to strip it away. Step-and-strip: step to create angles that give you leverage on their weapon, then pull or twist it away. Practice Schwertnehmen carefully with training weapons and protective gear, as these techniques involve close contact and weapon control. Start slowly to learn the mechanics, then gradually increase speed and resistance. Train the recognition of opportunities: not every moment allows Schwertnehmen—you must identify when their weapon is positioned favorably and when you have sufficient control to attempt disarming. Poor timing leads to failure or worse, losing your own weapon. Study historical sources for specific Schwertnehmen techniques: manuscripts show various specific disarms with details about gripping, leverage, and footwork. Practice these documented techniques as foundation for your close-range toolkit. Remember that disarming is high-reward (ends the fight decisively) but requires specific conditions (very close range, favorable weapon position, sufficient control). Don't force Schwertnehmen attempts when conditions aren't right. Schwertnehmen connects to broader principles of close-range combat: once you're at wrestling range, everything becomes viable—strikes, throws, disarms, locks. Use whatever technique the situation favors. Practice transitions: after successful Schwertnehmen, immediately follow with controlling actions (they may try to regain a weapon or close to unarmed grappling). Master Schwertnehmen and you add decisive disarming techniques to your close-range arsenal, able to end fights by removing your opponent's weapon when opportunities arise.
records.definition: Control/strip the opponent's weapon from contact.
records.briefDescription: Control/strip the opponent's weapon from contact.
records.fullDescription: Schwertnehmen (sword-taking, disarming) refers specifically to techniques for taking away or disarming your opponent's sword, typically executed at very close range as part of Ringen am Schwert (wrestling at the sword). These techniques involve controlling your opponent's weapon through leverage, joint manipulation, or force, then removing it from their grasp. Execute Schwertnehmen by: grabbing their blade or hilt with one or both hands while controlling it with your own sword; using leverage to force their weapon away from their body or out of their hands; applying joint locks to their wrist or arm that make holding their sword painful or impossible; trapping their sword against your body or using your crossguard to hook and control it; using two-hand advantage against their one hand by grabbing their hilt or blade with one of your hands while maintaining your own weapon; applying sudden force or torque that breaks their grip. The techniques often involve gripping their blade safely (at the flat or near the crossguard) or grabbing their hilt, then using mechanical advantage to twist, pull, or lever the sword away. Your own sword may be used to trap, hook, or control their weapon while your free hand performs the actual stripping motion. Some techniques involve stepping or body positioning that creates angles where their sword can be controlled and removed. Schwertnehmen typically requires very close range where you can reach their weapon with your hands, and often emerges from Ringen am Schwert situations where you're grappling with swords still in hand.
records.briefApplication: These techniques excel at decisive endings: without their weapon, your opponent is defeated (in training/competition) or at severe disadvantage (in historical context).

records.fullApplication: Use the short edge (Kurze Schneide) deliberately in techniques that specifically call for it, understanding that this back edge serves important tactical purposes in the longsword system. While the long edge is primary for most cuts, the short edge enables specific techniques and tactical options that expand your capabilities. The short edge appears in several key techniques: Schielhau often uses the short edge, particularly when delivered from certain angles—the blade rotates during the strike to present the short edge forward, allowing you to strike with specific mechanics that support the Schielhau's tactical purpose of breaking Pflug and countering thrusts. Zwerchhau from the right side frequently uses the short edge—as you strike horizontally from your right, rotating your hands brings the short edge forward, creating the characteristic high horizontal strike. Winding actions may rotate your blade to bring the short edge against your opponent's blade or toward targets, giving you additional options for edge orientation in the bind. Certain binding positions naturally place your short edge forward, and you can use this edge to control or press against your opponent's blade. Practice short edge techniques by focusing on the hand rotation required: when striking with the short edge, your hands must turn to present this edge forward, which feels different from true edge strikes. Your thumbs typically rotate toward the target (whereas with true edge, your knuckles rotate toward target). Drill the specific techniques that use short edge: practice Schielhau with proper hand rotation to deliver the short edge; practice Zwerchhau from right side with short edge; practice winding in the bind that transitions between edges. Develop edge awareness: know at all times which edge is forward and be able to transition between edges deliberately through proper winding and rotation. The short edge teaches an important principle: a double-edged sword gives you two edges to work with, expanding your tactical options beyond single-edge weapons. Don't limit yourself to only the long edge—use both edges as techniques demand. Historical sources specifically mention short edge techniques and positions, indicating this was a deliberate and important aspect of longsword technique, not an afterthought. Some techniques work better or only work with specific edges—respect these technical requirements by using the correct edge. Practice edge control: in all binding and winding work, maintain awareness of which edge is engaged with your opponent's blade and which edge is threatening openings. This awareness lets you choose appropriate techniques based on current edge orientation. Remember that while most basic cuts use the long edge for simplicity and power, advanced techniques frequently employ the short edge for specific tactical purposes. Master both edges and you have complete technical control of your sword, able to strike and work effectively with whichever edge the situation favors.
records.definition: Opposite of true edge; key in Schielhau/windings.
records.briefDescription: Opposite of true edge; key in Schielhau/windings.
records.fullDescription: Kurze Schneide (short edge, false edge, back edge) refers to the edge of the longsword blade that faces away from you when you hold the sword in a normal grip, opposite the Lange Schneide (long edge/true edge). On a double-edged longsword, this is the edge that would face backward if you held the sword with the true edge forward. The short edge is called 'short' not because of its physical length but because it's on the 'short' or back side of the blade relative to your hand position and body. In a standard grip with quillons horizontal, the short edge is the one facing upward (toward your thumb if using thumb grip). The short edge is used for specific cuts and techniques where you strike with the back of the blade rather than the primary edge. Important applications of the short edge include: the Schielhau (squinting strike) which is typically delivered with the short edge from certain positions; certain Zwerchhau (thwart strike) variations, particularly when striking from the right side; various winding actions that rotate the blade to bring the short edge into play; some binding and parrying positions that use the short edge to control the opponent's blade. Using the short edge typically requires rotating your hands and wrists to present this edge forward. When cutting with the short edge, your hand position and body mechanics differ from true edge cuts—often involving more wrist rotation and different body angles.
records.briefApplication: Use the short edge (Kurze Schneide) deliberately in techniques that specifically call for it, understanding that this back edge serves important tactical purposes in the longsword system.

records.fullApplication: Use the long edge (Lange Schneide) as your primary cutting edge for most techniques, understanding that this edge represents your natural, powerful, and structurally sound option for the majority of longsword work. The long edge should be your default for most situations because it offers mechanical advantages: natural alignment with your body structure, powerful cutting mechanics, strong defensive positions, and intuitive edge orientation. Most fundamental techniques use the long edge: all basic Oberhau (descending cuts) use the long edge; most Unterhau (rising cuts) use the long edge; many Mittelhau (middle cuts) use the long edge; the Zornhau uses the long edge; the Scheitelhau uses the long edge (the Krumphau, or Crooked Cut, by contrast is thrown with the short or 'crooked' edge). When binding, the long edge forward gives you strong structure and good control options. When parrying with techniques like Absetzen, the long edge provides solid interception of incoming attacks. Practice edge awareness: know that your long edge is forward most of the time and develop strong technique with this edge before worrying excessively about short edge techniques. Master the fundamentals: powerful cutting with the long edge, strong binding with the long edge, effective parrying with the long edge. These are the foundation of longsword technique. The long edge also provides advantages in edge alignment: because it's naturally aligned with your knuckles, you can use your knuckle position as a guide to ensure proper edge orientation during cuts—if your knuckles are aimed at the target, your long edge is likely aligned correctly. When practicing cuts, focus on long edge mechanics: lead with your knuckles, keep your forearms relatively aligned (not twisted), drive the edge through the target with body rotation and extension. These mechanics create powerful, clean cuts that utilize the long edge effectively. The historical sources primarily describe long edge techniques, with short edge techniques appearing in specific special applications. This indicates that the long edge was considered primary, with the short edge as supplementary. When binding with the long edge forward, you have strong structure and can press effectively, wind to bring your point online, or maintain control. This is why most binding work defaults to long edge engagement. Practice defending with the long edge: techniques like Absetzen specifically use long edge to intercept and control incoming attacks, combining defense and offense effectively. The long edge gives you strong structure for this simultaneous defend-and-threaten approach. Remember that while the short edge has important specific uses, the long edge remains your primary tool for most situations. Develop strong long edge technique as foundation, then add short edge techniques as refinements that expand your tactical options. Master the long edge and you master the core of longsword technique: powerful cuts, strong bindings, effective defenses, all built on mechanically sound use of your primary cutting edge.
records.definition: Main edge for most cuts and strong parries.
records.briefDescription: Main edge for most cuts and strong parries.
records.fullDescription: Lange Schneide (long edge, true edge, primary edge) refers to the edge of the longsword blade that faces forward when you hold the sword in a normal grip, aligned with your knuckles and naturally positioned for cutting. On a double-edged longsword, this is the edge that faces toward your target when you hold the sword ready to strike. The long edge is called 'long' not because of its physical length but because it's on the 'long' or forward side of the blade relative to your hand position and body—it's the edge you naturally lead with. In a standard grip with quillons horizontal, the long edge is the one facing downward (toward your knuckles if using standard grip). The long edge is the primary cutting edge used for most techniques: the majority of cuts (Oberhau, Unterhau, Mittelhau) are delivered with the long edge; most defensive positions and parries use the long edge to control the opponent's blade; binding and winding work often maintains long edge forward; cuts like the Zornhau (Wrath Cut) and Scheitelhau (Scalp Cut) are delivered with the long edge, whereas the Krumphau (Crooked Cut) characteristically uses the short edge—Meyer even names the short edge the 'crooked edge.' Using the long edge is mechanically natural and powerful because it aligns with your body structure and delivers force effectively. When cutting with the long edge, your knuckles lead the strike, your forearms remain relatively untwisted, and your body mechanics support powerful edge-on-target impact. The long edge provides the strongest structure for parrying because it aligns with your hand and arm position naturally.
records.briefApplication: Use the long edge as your default cutting and parrying edge for most of Meyer's cuts and bindings, reserving the short edge for the techniques that specifically call for it.

records.fullApplication: Use the point (Ort) chiefly to threaten and control in the bind, remembering that Meyer's longsword favors the cut. The earlier tradition made the thrust the finishing tool ('the point threatens and finishes'), but Meyer sets the thrust largely aside in the longsword—he defers Ochs, Pflug, and the thrusts to his rapier—so most of your finishing is done with cuts and slices, not the point. Where the point still earns its place: In the bind, wind to bring your point online toward an opening while keeping blade contact—the winding system revolves around keeping the point threatening as you feel (Fuhlen) whether the opponent is hard or soft. In setting off (Absetzen), extend your point to displace an incoming cut or thrust while simultaneously threatening in return; after any parry your point can immediately seek an opening. From the high windings out of Ochs, and from Pflug, a thrust to the face or chest is available when the opening appears and the situation (earnest combat rather than the Fechtschule) allows it. Practice point control: your point should be stable, directed, and online even as your body moves, so that a threat or a thrust is available instantly when it is warranted. Use the point to control distance and the centerline—extending it forward (as in Langort or the Speaking Window) creates a barrier the opponent must deal with before reaching you, buying you tempo. But do not fall into a thrust-centric habit: in Meyer's longsword the point sets up and threatens while the cut, the slice, and the handwork of the bind do most of the decisive work; convert readily from a point threat into a cut or slice when the thrust is closed off or forbidden. Remember Meyer's own note that in the fencing of his day the thrust had largely fallen out of use with the longsword—train the point as a threatening and setting-off tool that supports your cutting game, not as the heart of the system.
records.definition: The point or tip of the blade; Meyer largely sets the thrust aside in the longsword, but the point still threatens in the bind through winding and setting-off (Absetzen).
records.briefDescription: The point or tip of the blade; Meyer largely sets the thrust aside in the longsword, but the point still threatens in the bind through winding and setting-off (Absetzen).
records.fullDescription: Ort (point, tip) refers to the pointed end of the longsword blade. In the earlier Liechtenauer tradition the point was the central threatening and finishing tool, but Meyer's 1570 longsword deliberately de-emphasizes the thrust: he states that the thrust 'in our present time is not in the fencing,' and reserves detailed thrusting—together with the guards Ochs and Pflug—for his rapier section, since thrusts were banned in the Fechtschule and restricted by civic law. In Meyer's longsword the cut is primary and the point is used more sparingly. Even so, the point remains important: it threatens in the bind, where winding brings it online toward an opening while blade contact is maintained; it is used to set off (Absetzen) an incoming attack while threatening in return; and where a thrust does appear—in the high windings from Ochs, from Pflug, or in earnest combat—the point finishes. Good point control means keeping the point stable, online, and directed, not wavering or wandering offline during your actions. Because a thrust travels a straight line rather than an arc it arrives quickly when it is used, but in the sportive longsword you will more often threaten with the point and convert to a cut or slice than drive the thrust home.
records.briefApplication: Use the point to threaten and set off (Absetzen) in the bind and to finish where a thrust is called for, remembering that Meyer's longsword favors the cut over the thrust.

records.briefDescription: The strong half of the blade nearest the hilt, used to bind, parry, and dominate the opponent's Weak.
records.fullDescription: Stärke (the Strong; Meyer's 'Sterck') is the half of the blade nearest the hilt, from roughly the middle down to the cross. Meyer counts the Weak and the Strong among the fundamental parts of the sword and divides the blade into the Strong (nearest the hilt) and the Weak (nearest the point), with the haft—grip, cross, and pommel—behind the Strong. Because it sits close to your hands, the Strong has the greatest leverage and mechanical advantage: a bind made with your Strong is powerful and hard to displace. You catch and parry incoming cuts on the Strong of your blade, and in the bind your Strong controls the opponent's blade, especially when it meets their Weak, where your leverage is greatest. Feeling (Fühlen) whether the opponent is hard or soft in the bind, and the choice to hold firm (Hart) or yield (Weich), both depend on this division of the blade into Strong and Weak.
records.briefApplication: Bind, parry, and press with your Strong—especially against the opponent's Weak—where your leverage lets you dominate the bind.
records.fullApplication: Use the Stärke whenever you need power and control in contact. Catch a strong incoming cut on the Strong of your blade, where it is hard for the opponent to force through. In the bind, seek to place your Strong against the opponent's Weak: from there your superior leverage lets you press their blade aside, wind, or work to an opening while they can do little. This strong-against-weak relationship underlies Meyer's handwork—when you feel (Fühlen) that the opponent is hard or soft, you decide with your Strong whether to hold firm (Hart) and overpower, or to yield (Weich) and let their force run past into a slice or a change. Conversely, avoid binding your Weak against their Strong, where you will be overpowered. Remember that leverage shifts along the blade: the nearer to your cross the contact sits, the stronger you are, so step and wind to keep the contact on your Strong when you want to dominate, and drive the work from there.

records.briefDescription: The weak half of the blade nearest the point—quick and far-reaching, but with little leverage in the bind.
records.fullDescription: Schwäche (the Weak; Meyer's 'Schwech') is the half of the blade nearest the point, from roughly the middle up to the tip. Meyer names the Weak and the Strong among the fundamental parts of the sword: the blade divides into the Strong (nearest the hilt) and the Weak (nearest the point). Having little leverage, the Weak is easily dominated in a bind—if the opponent catches your Weak on their Strong, they command the bind. Its virtue is speed and reach: the Weak is the part that lands the cut and the slice, that flicks and snaps to distant openings, and that you throw at the opponent's head or arms in quick actions. Because binding Weak-on-Strong leaves you overpowered, much of Meyer's handwork is about winning the leverage contest—getting your Strong onto the opponent's Weak while keeping your own Weak free to strike.
records.briefApplication: Strike and slice with your Weak for speed and reach, but avoid binding it against the opponent's Strong, where you will be overpowered.
records.fullApplication: Use the Schwäche for everything that needs speed and reach rather than leverage: the Weak is what actually lands your cuts and slices, snaps to the head or arms, and flicks to distant openings. In the bind, be aware that your Weak is vulnerable—if the opponent gets their Strong onto it, they dominate, and you should not try to out-push them there. Instead, when you find yourself Weak against their Strong, yield (Weich): let their pressure run off, and change through, wind, or slice to an opening rather than fighting the leverage. Offensively, aim to bind or catch with your Strong against their Weak, then strike them with your Weak to the nearest opening. Meyer's provocations often reach the opponent's Weak first ('bind on him in front, in his Weak, with your point') to unsettle it before working in. Understanding the Strong/Weak division is essential to feeling (Fühlen) and to every hard-or-soft decision in the bind.

records.briefDescription: The crossguard of the sword—part of the hilt (Gehilz)—used to guard the hands, to catch and hang off cuts, and to hook, trap, or strike at close range.
records.fullDescription: The Kreuz (cross or crossguard) is the transverse bar between grip and blade; together with the grip and pommel it forms the hilt, which Meyer calls the Gehilz. Meyer treats the haft—grip, cross, and pommel—as one of the working parts of the sword, and the cross does real work in the longsword: it protects the hands in the bind, it can be raised overhead ('drive up with your hilt above your head') to catch and hang off a descending cut while your point or short edge stays online, and at close quarters you reach over or hook with the cross and pommel to trap the opponent's blade or arm. In crossed-hands cuts and in the windings, the orientation of the cross—set horizontal or driven forward—governs how strongly you bind and how well your hands are covered.
records.briefApplication: Raise the hilt to catch cuts and cover the hands, and use the cross to hook, trap, or strike in the bind and at close range.
records.fullApplication: Use the Gehilz actively, not just as a handle. When a strong cut comes in high, drive your hilt up above your head with the cross set horizontal to catch and hang off it, covering your hands while your point or short edge remains online. In the bind, keep the cross oriented to shield your hands and to press—setting the cross forward strengthens your structure. At close quarters and in running in, the cross and pommel become tools: reach over the opponent's arms with your hilt, hook their blade or wrist with the cross, or grip the blade and lever with the cross for a disarm or throw. Meyer also uses hilt strikes to the face at close range. Always be aware of where your cross points, because it determines whether your hands are covered and how much leverage you can bring against the opponent's blade.

records.briefDescription: The weighted knob at the base of the hilt (standard HEMA also Knauf), used to counterbalance the blade, steer the point in the windings, hook over the arms, and strike or wrench at close range.
records.fullDescription: The Knopf (pommel; standard HEMA also Knauf) is the weighted knob at the base of the grip that counterbalances the blade. Meyer counts the pommel among the working parts of the haft. Beyond balancing the sword, the pommel is a functional tool in the handwork: you turn the pommel through in the windings to redirect your point and edge; you drive the pommel over the opponent's arm to trap or lever it; and in running in and grappling you release a hand, grip the blade, and use the pommel to hook, wrench, or strike. At very close range the pommel serves as an impact tool to the face or body. Because it sits behind your hands, moving the pommel is how you steer the point and manage leverage in the bind.
records.briefApplication: Turn and drive the pommel to steer your point in the windings, to hook over the opponent's arm, and to strike or wrench at close range.
records.fullApplication: Use the Knopf as a lever and a hook, not just a counterweight. In winding, turning the pommel through under or over the bind is what brings your point and edge back online while you keep contact. When you have bound and want to control the opponent's arms, drive your pommel over or through above their arm and wrench downward to trap or off-balance them. In running in and Ringen am Schwert, release your left hand, grip your own blade (as in a half-sword) or reach with the pommel to hook the opponent's arm, hilt, or neck, and use it to wrench their weapon or set up a throw. At the closest range the heavy pommel is an impact weapon to the face or body. Throughout, remember that steering the pommel is how you steer the point: small movements of the pommel produce large movements of the tip, so use it deliberately to keep your point threatening and your leverage favorable.

Use the Failer (Fehler) as one of Meyer's central deceptive devices: provoke a reaction, fail your cut, and strike the opening it leaves. Unlike a purely committed style, Meyer's cut-based Fechtschule game leans heavily on feints and deception—he names the Failer and the Double Failer (Doppelfehler) and devotes a section to them—so this is a core tool, not a rare exception. Fehlen works when: your opponent is defensive and prone to parrying, making them susceptible to feints that draw their parry; you need to open a specific line that is currently defended; or you want to read their reactions and defensive patterns. Execute Fehlen by making your initial cut appear genuine and threatening enough that they must respond—if they don't believe it, they won't react and the technique fails. Cut with apparent commitment toward one opening, causing them to move to defend that line, then let the cut fail and run past and strike the line they have now opened. Common Failer applications include: Feint high, strike low: begin a strong cut toward the head to make them raise their defense, then let it fail and cut low to the opening they leave. Feint one side, strike the other: begin a cut to one side to draw the parry, then fail and strike or slice to the opposite side; Meyer's Double Failer chains this—fail on one side, wind around the blade, and fail again before landing on the far opening. The Squinter as a feint: squint 'with the face' as if to cut one line, let the short-edge cut fail, and swing in with the Weak to the true opening. Feint to provoke Nachreisen (chasing): deliberately fall short so they try to chase or counter your 'miss,' then strike them during that attempt. Practice making feints convincing: your initial cut must look real enough that a skilled opponent reacts to it—half-hearted feints waste time and tempo. Commit as if it were real, changing only at the last moment when their reaction appears. Meyer himself notes that double failing 'requires an experienced fighter,' so drill the timing and blade control until you can fail and redirect cleanly rather than flailing. Remember that good opponents may not take the bait or may respond unexpectedly, and that against a fighter who has learned to ignore your feints, a genuine committed cut becomes the surprise. Master the Failer as a developed part of your handwork—deployed deliberately to solve defensive problems and keep the opponent guessing—rather than as an occasional afterthought.
records.definition: A purposeful miss to provoke and change through.
records.briefDescription: A purposeful miss to provoke and change through.
records.fullDescription: Fehlen (feinting, missing, failing) refers to deliberately missing or shortening an attack to provoke a reaction from your opponent, then exploiting that reaction by changing to a different attack. This is a deceptive technique where your apparent attack is actually a setup for your real attack. Execute Fehlen by beginning a strike that appears committed and threatening, causing your opponent to react (typically by moving to parry that line), but intentionally let the cut fail and run past just before it lands, then immediately strike to a different opening they have now exposed. The key is making the initial attack appear genuine enough that they must react, while keeping enough control to redirect instantly. Your feint must be convincing: if they don't react because they recognize it as a feint, the technique fails. Meyer names this device the Failer (Fehler) and treats it as an artful, developed technique, devoting a section to both single and double Failers—the Doppelfehler (Double Failer), where you fail on one side, wind around the blade, and fail again before striking the true opening. The feint runs closely with Meyer's other deceptions: the Squinter (Schielhau), for instance, is often thrown as a feint 'with the face,' squinting as if to cut one line and then failing and striking another. Feinting is thus a prominent, valued part of Meyer's cut-based Fechtschule system, not a marginal tactic—though Meyer notes that double failing 'requires an experienced fighter,' so it rewards timing and blade control rather than random flailing.
records.briefApplication: Use the Failer to bait a parry, then let the cut fail and strike the opening it leaves—one of Meyer's core deceptive devices in the handwork.
